items.title: Add precision alignment workflow with session calibration, reversal correction, and refreshed UI renders
items.body:
This expands Evanline from a single-reading angle viewer into a session-based measurement workflow optimized for repeatability. It adds device / fixture / session calibration, multi-point baseline capture, reversal-aware measurement correction, and reporting that surfaces whether a session is trustworthy enough for comparison or adjustment.

- **Precision workflow**
  - Adds a Quick vs Precision split in the main UI.
  - Introduces a guided session flow for:
    - device reference capture
    - fixture selection
    - baseline establishment
    - repeated wheel captures
    - reversal checks
    - trust-gated save/reporting

- **Session calibration model**
  - Extends persisted state with:
    - device profile
    - named fixture profiles
    - FL / FR / RL / RR baseline points
    - per-wheel forward / reverse capture sets
    - repeatability and trust metadata
  - Migrates legacy local state forward into the new storage shape.

- **Measurement and correction logic**
  - Adds repeat-capture scoring based on cross-capture agreement instead of a single settled sample.
  - Uses forward/reverse capture pairs to estimate mounting bias and compute a reversal-corrected value.
  - Applies baseline compensation from around-the-car Level measurements before reporting the final value.

- **Reporting and saved results**
  - Precision saves now store:
    - raw forward value
    - reversal-corrected value
    - final reported value
    - reversal bias
    - capture count
    - baseline quality
    - trust verdict
  - Saved reading summaries now distinguish quick snapshots from precision-session results.

- **Guidance and product framing**
  - Updates in-app instructions and README to reflect the fixture-first workflow, around-car baseline capture, and reversible 3-point jig guidance.
  - Frames the app as a calibrated comparative tool focused on same-car / same-jig / same-floor repeatability.

- **UI renders**
  - Refreshes the screenshots in `/renders` to match the updated guided workflow and precision UI.

```js
const reversalBias = forward && reverse ? (forward.mean + reverse.mean) / 2 : null;
const reversalCorrectedValue = forward && reverse
  ? (forward.mean - reverse.mean) / 2
  : forwardOnlyValue;
const finalValue = Number.isFinite(reversalCorrectedValue)
  ? reversalCorrectedValue - baselineComp
  : null;
```

items.title: feat: add LDBC SNB Interactive short-read benchmark (Lane 1)
items.body:
First lane of the real-workload benchmark program: the LDBC SNB Interactive short-read queries (IS1-IS7), run against four engines under a shared fairness harness, at both SF1 and SF10 scale.

- **New `packages/benchmarks/src/real/`**: schema (`schema/snb-graph.ts`), dataset streaming reader (`dataset/ldbc-csv.ts`) + a tiny committed smoke fixture, four engine drivers (`engines/typegraph-sqlite.ts`, `typegraph-postgres.ts`, `neo4j.ts`, `ladybug.ts`), and a lane-agnostic harness (`harness/`: stats with CV-based noisy-sample flagging, value-level parity gate, competitor doctor, `summary.json` writer, `history.jsonl` appender).
- **TypeGraph engines drive IS1-IS7 entirely through the query builder** — no hand-written SQL (`engines/typegraph-queries.ts`'s module doc explains the `.prepare()`/`.execute()` fairness rationale and the `Message` ontological-supertype workaround for the polymorphic `replyOf` edge).
- **Neo4j and LadybugDB launch imperatively** (docker run + tmpfs / in-process embedded) and implement the same 7 queries in native Cypher, using their own native handling of polymorphic node/edge types (multi-label nodes, multi-pair `REL TABLE`s) instead of TypeGraph's ontology workaround.
- **New `packages/benchmarks/src/real/ec2/`**: an EC2 runner (`docs/ec2-benchmark-runner.md`) so SF1/SF10 can run on a dedicated, ephemeral cloud instance instead of local hardware. SSM Run Command is the default, no-key-pair control channel; generic enough for anyone who clones the repo to point at their own AWS account. An opt-in `--ssh-public-key-path` diagnostic fallback exists for when SSM itself is what's broken. Hardened over five rounds of review — see below.
- **CI-safe**: `bench:snb:smoke:check` runs the tiny fixture end-to-end; a competitor-doctor preflight reports missing Docker/packages as explicit failed rows (never silent), and the run stays green with 0 or 1 runnable engines — it only fails on a genuine parity mismatch (row count or value digest) between 2+ engines that actually ran.
- **Incidental fix**: the root `.gitignore`'s unscoped `reports/` rule (meant for Stryker mutation-testing output) had been silently excluding `packages/benchmarks/reports/history.jsonl` from every commit since it was introduced — scoped to `packages/typegraph/reports/` so both the existing synthetic perf suite's history and this lane's history are actually committed going forward.

**One `packages/typegraph` change**: `walAutocheckpointPages`, a new `createLocalSqliteBackend` pragma option (see "SF10" below for why). This branch and `main` independently arrived at the same fix; `main`'s version (merged separately as #251, with an upper-bound validation this branch's original commit didn't have) is now what this branch carries after reconciling with `main` — see "`main` reconciliation" below. Everything else is benchmarks-only; three other library fixes were needed along the way but each landed separately in its own PR (#226, #227).

## Review history: 5 rounds, all fixed and re-verified with a fresh EC2 run

Five rounds of review found issues serious enough that no query-latency number from before this PR's fixes could be trusted. All findings below are fixed; a fresh SF1 + SF10 EC2 run on the fully-fixed commit (`2bc7f74f`) has since replaced every invalidated number — see [Results](#results) below.

### Round 1 (6 findings)

1. **IS2 implemented the wrong workload, in all three engine drivers.** Checked against the official LDBC reference Cypher (`ldbc/ldbc_snb_interactive_v1_impls`): IS2 is "recent messages of a person" — the *given* person's own messages, tie-broken `messageId ASC`. This PR's drivers traversed to that person's *friends* and measured messages *they* authored, tie-broken `DESC` — a materially different, heavier workload. Every engine shared the identical mistake, which is exactly why row-count parity never caught it. Fixed in `typegraph-queries.ts`, `neo4j.ts`, and `ladybug.ts`.
2. **`materializeIndexes()`'s best-effort result was silently discarded** in both the SQLite and Postgres drivers. Fixed: `assertMessageIndexMaterialized()` (`schema/snb-graph.ts`) checks the result and throws if the index wasn't created or already materialized.
3. **`collect()` (`run-sf1-ec2.ts`) extracted the benchmark's exit code but never checked it.** Fixed: throws (after writing whatever partial artifacts exist) on non-`Success` SSM status, a missing exit-code marker, or a nonzero exit code.
4. **`--profile=sf10` always defaulted to `c7i.4xlarge`**, the same 32GB instance type that OOM'd on four separate SF10 attempts. Fixed: profile-aware default (`r7i.4xlarge` for `sf10`); `--instance-type` still overrides explicitly.
5. **Neo4j's `snb_post_id`/`snb_comment_id` constraints had no current query-time consumer** (every by-id match goes through the shared `:Message` label). Fixed: removed.
6. **Release-facing copy didn't match the branch** (stale "no typegraph changes," "fastest across the board" overclaim, a nonexistent script reference, a stale "no direct measurement" line). Fixed throughout the results doc, the EC2 guide, and this PR body.

### Round 2 (5 more findings — the smoke run in round 1 proved *execution and row-count parity*, not LDBC *semantic* parity)

1. **IS2 was still incomplete after round 1's fix.** The official query also returns message content and root-post-author names; TypeGraph omitted content, Neo4j and LadybugDB omitted both content and author names. IDs were also tie-broken with plain `localeCompare` (`"message:10"` sorting before `"message:2"`) despite official ids being numeric. Fixed: content + names added to all three engines' IS2; a shared `compareIdsAscending()` helper (`engines/types.ts`) makes every id tie-break numeric-aware.
2. **IS3/IS5/IS6/IS7 weren't equivalent across engines either**, and row-count-only parity could never have caught any of it: TypeGraph's IS3 had no defined ordering at all; Neo4j's and LadybugDB's IS6 omitted forum id/title; TypeGraph's and LadybugDB's IS7 omitted reply content and author names. Fixed: every query across all three engines now returns exactly the official LDBC output fields, correctly ordered.
3. **The parity gate itself only ever compared row counts.** Upgraded to a value-level canonical digest per row (`SnbQueryResult.digest`, `canonicalDigest()` in `engines/types.ts`, `harness/parity.ts`) — engines can no longer agree on count while disagreeing on field values, omitted fields, or order. Verified on the smoke fixture: this immediately caught one real remaining bug (TypeGraph's IS3 digest used the field name `personId`, Neo4j/LadybugDB used `id` — same values, incomparable digests) before landing at all 7 queries passing true value-level parity across all four engines.
4. **A successful SSM command with no results could still report success** (`resultsText === "{}"` didn't feed the failure predicate). Fixed: `!hasParseableResults` added to `collect()`'s failure check.
5. **Failed runs could contaminate canonical history** — `reports/history.jsonl` was appended before validating the run succeeded. Fixed: raw history lines are always preserved locally (run-scoped, not shared) for post-mortem; the *canonical* file is only appended after every success condition passes. A related, smaller finding — four smoke-test history rows this session accidentally generated recorded a git SHA that didn't contain the uncommitted fixes producing them — was caught and reverted, not committed.
6. **(P2) Neo4j's fairness label still described the just-removed Post/Comment constraints**, and the results doc claimed Neo4j's load time was unaffected by round 1's fixes when constraint creation actually runs inside its timed `load()`. Both fixed.

### Round 3 (2 more P1s — round 2's own IS2 fix wasn't actually correctness-proof — plus 3 P2s)

1. **Round 2's `IS2_CANDIDATE_LIMIT` buffer (a fixed-size native `LIMIT` re-sorted numerically in JS) wasn't provably correct.** Confirmed with a concrete counter-example: a same-`creationDate` tie cluster larger than the buffer (e.g. 30 messages sharing one timestamp, ids 1-30) causes the native lexicographic `LIMIT` to exclude genuinely-top-10 candidates (numeric ids 3-9) before the JS resort ever sees them — even a *correct* numeric resort of a *wrong* candidate set produces a wrong answer. Fixed by removing the native `LIMIT` entirely across all three engines: IS2 now fetches all of a person's own messages (unlimited), sorts numerically, and slices to 10 purely in JS — correct regardless of tie-cluster size.
2. **`collect()`'s success predicate still didn't require a parseable `summary.json` or non-empty `history.jsonl` lines** — only `results.json` was checked. Fixed: `hasParseableSummary`/`hasHistoryLines` added alongside the existing checks; a run is only "successful" when all three reproducibility artifacts are present.
3. **(P2) Stale "row-count parity" wording** throughout `cli.ts`, `request-plan.ts`, `snb-short-reads.ts`'s console output, the README, and the results doc — corrected to describe both row-count and value-digest parity, matching round 2's actual gate upgrade.
4. **(P2) README's SF1 load-time numbers were pre-fix stale** (75-80 min) — updated to the current numbers (SQLite ~40 min, Postgres ~12 min).
5. **(P2) Neo4j's loader was described as "batched UNWIND ... IN TRANSACTIONS"** in both the README and results doc when it's actually the offline `neo4j-admin database import` — corrected in both places. Also softened the lane's "official LDBC" framing: the README now explicitly names the two relationships this schema deliberately flattens into properties (`Person.cityId`, `Forum.moderatorId`) instead of modeling as edges, and calls the lane "LDBC SNB-derived" rather than a full schema-conformance claim — the query *fields and ordering* are still verified against the official reference; the schema-shape simplification is a separate, honestly-disclosed thing.

### Round 4 (2 more P1s — round 3's own IS2 fix traded correctness for a new fairness problem)

1. **Round 3's fix (removing IS2's native `LIMIT` entirely) was correctness-proof but changed the measured workload.** The official query applies its own `ORDER BY messageCreationDate DESC, messageId ASC LIMIT 10` *engine-side*, before the root-post-author walk. Fetching every message a person ever authored instead — every engine, unconditionally — transferred full message content over the network for engines that pay a real round trip (Postgres, Neo4j), disproportionately penalizing them versus the embedded engines, and diverged from official semantics. The repo's own index documentation notes some IS2 candidate pools run to thousands of rows, so this wasn't a theoretical concern. Root-caused properly instead of patched again: `dataset/ldbc-csv.ts` now zero-pads every id's numeric portion to a fixed width, so a plain lexicographic `ORDER BY id ASC` (SQL or Cypher alike) already agrees with numeric order, for any tie-cluster size — this is what actually broke in round 2/3, not the presence of a `LIMIT` per se. With that fixed, native `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` is restored everywhere: TypeGraph/LadybugDB fetch each of Post/Comment's own top 10 and merge (any message in the true top 10 of the union must be in its own type's top 10 too, so this is provably equal to the true top 10, for any candidate-pool or tie-cluster size, transferring at most 20 rows regardless of how many messages the person actually authored); Neo4j's unified `:Message` label needs only one query.
   - Also added: `bench:snb:verify-is2-tie-break`, an adversarial correctness oracle independent of cross-engine consensus. Every engine agreeing has already gone wrong twice in this lane (the friend-workload bug, the lexicographic-tie-break bug) — consensus alone doesn't prove correctness. The smoke fixture now includes a dedicated person who authors 25 same-creationDate comments; with no other tie-breaking signal, that person's correct IS2 answer (the cluster's 10 smallest message ids) is knowable in advance, and the new script checks each doctor-runnable engine's actual result against that known answer directly. All 4 engines pass.
2. **The paid EC2 path could still report success with fewer than the full four-engine set.** Doctor-unavailable engines are filtered out of the run rather than recorded as a failure — correct behavior for a local/CI invocation (a no-Docker environment should still exit 0 on the two embedded engines), wrong for a run whose entire point is a complete four-engine comparison: a container failing to start on the instance would silently produce a smaller-than-requested but still "successful" run. Fixed: `collect()` now parses `results.json.engines` and requires all four canonical engine names to be present before declaring success, and additionally fetches + preserves `competitor-doctor.json` locally (success or failure) so an incomplete run is diagnosable without re-connecting to the instance.

### Round 5 (1 more P1 — round 4's own new oracle test didn't actually test anything)

1. **The tie-break oracle's 25 tie-cluster ids were one contiguous 3-digit range (120..144)**, so unpadded lexicographic order and numeric order coincide by construction — same-length numeral strings always compare identically both ways. The check would pass whether or not `dataset/ldbc-csv.ts`'s zero-padding fix was actually applied, catching nothing; it was consensus theater dressed up as an oracle. Fixed: split into two blocks of different digit widths (3-digit `120..129`, 4-digit `1000..1014`) — unpadded lexicographic order now ranks every 4-digit id ahead of every 3-digit one (`"1000" < "120"` character-by-character), so an unpadded engine returns the wrong answer (`1000..1009`) instead of the true one (`120..129`). Verified directly, not just reasoned about: temporarily reverted the padding fix, confirmed all 4 engines fail with exactly that predicted wrong answer, then restored it and confirmed all 4 pass again.

## Results

Full writeup: `packages/benchmarks/reports/snb-lane1-results.md`. Both scales below are fresh runs on commit `2bc7f74f` (every fix from all 5 rounds in place): **0 engine failures, 7/7 queries at full value-level digest parity** (not row-count alone) at both scales. Single run each — not yet a publishable comparison per the program plan's multi-run bar (tracked in the results doc's Next steps).

### SF1 (9,892 persons, 1,003,605 posts, 2,052,169 comments) — 7/7 `comparable=yes`, 0 failures

| Engine | Load time |
| --- | --- |
| ladybugdb | 41.6 s |
| neo4j | 71.4 s (1.2 min) |
| typegraph-postgres | 669.3 s (11.2 min) |
| typegraph-sqlite | 587.1 s (9.8 min) |

SQLite and Neo4j both load dramatically faster than the last SF1 run reported in this PR (SQLite ~4.1x, Neo4j ~4.3x) — not a new optimization, but the SF10 investigation's covering-index-deferral and constraint-removal fixes finally showing up in an SF1 number for the first time (that run predates both). Postgres and LadybugDB, whose load paths weren't touched by either fix, measured 3.5% and 22.7% faster than the previous run, respectively — cross-commit observations that can't establish run-to-run variance or causality on their own. See the results doc for the full query-latency table (IS2 still dominates every engine's latency, as structurally expected — a top-10 selection plus a per-message root-post-author walk).

### SF10 (65,645 persons, 7,435,696 posts, 21,865,475 comments) — 7/7 `comparable=yes`, 0 failures

Getting one clean, *fast* SF10 run originally took eight EC2 attempts across two root-causing efforts — a memory-exhaustion failure disguised as a networking problem (attempts 1-5), then an EBS gp3 volume's default IOPS ceiling that made a correctly-implemented, locally-validated SQLite checkpoint-tuning fix show zero real-world improvement (attempts 6-8). Full narrative in the results doc. This run is on commit `2bc7f74f` (all 5 review rounds); attempt 8 above was commit `a58ae38e` (load-time fixes only, predating those rounds) — a consistent second load-time data point, not the same commit:

| Engine | Load time |
| --- | --- |
| ladybugdb | 354.0 s (5.9 min, +10.7% vs. attempt 8) |
| neo4j | 404.2 s (6.7 min, +8.8%) |
| typegraph-postgres | 7,127.5 s (1.98 h, +7.4%) |
| typegraph-sqlite | 10,929.4 s (3.04 h, -2.1%, i.e. faster) |

The second run differed by -2.1% to +10.7% across engines. These provide a consistent second load-time point, but two cross-commit observations do not establish run-to-run variance or causality — the two runs are on different commits, so a small, real, commit-attributable effect can't be ruled out from two samples alone. With a fresh SF1 run now available under the identical (`2bc7f74f`) fixes, the results doc also derives a fair SF1-to-SF10 growth-rate comparison for the first time: Postgres grows almost exactly linearly with the ~10.65x comment-count increase; SQLite grows noticeably super-linearly (~18.6x), consistent with the documented `wal_autocheckpoint` tuning's own caveat that it "holds through roughly 50,000-100,000 pages, then regresses again" — worth a deeper look if pursued further, not investigated in this PR.

items.title: Add OPC UA - Vision companion spec (machine + robotics vision, AI on/off server); UsdGeomCameraType, Isaac Sim annexes, optional Data Channels media transport
items.body:
## What this PR changes or proposes

Adds **`OPC UA — Vision`**, a new companion specification under `metaverse-specs/vision/` (namespace `http://opcfoundation.org/UA/Vision/`), covering **machine vision and robotics vision** in one model, with AI integration both on- and off-server.

It also makes two additive changes to the existing OpenUSD specs so the new model has somewhere concrete to attach.

**New — `metaverse-specs/vision/`**

- `OPC-UA-Vision.md` — the normative spec (§1–13 plus Annexes A–E)
- `OPC-UA-Vision-Research.md` — the research report that justifies it, committed **beside the spec** and linked relatively
- Generated `Opc.Ua.Vision.NodeSet2.xml` + `NodeIds.csv` (278 nodes, 56 types) from `extras/vision/tools/build_model.py`
- `validate_local.py`, registered in `metaverse-specs/validate_all.py`
- Two worked examples — robotics (eye-in-hand picking) and machine-vision inspection — **generated** from JSON descriptors by `build_examples.py`, published both as **Annex F** and **Annex G** of the spec and standalone beside their overlays

**Changed — OpenUSD Part 2 (`openusd-scene`)**

- Adds **`UsdGeomCameraType : UsdGeomXformableType`** (`FocalLength`, `HorizontalAperture`, `VerticalAperture`, aperture offsets, `ClippingRange`, `FStop`, `FocusDistance`, `Projection`, `Exposure`). The materialized UsdGeom subset previously had **no camera prim type** at all.
- NodeIds are **appended** (type `1024`, members `6078+`), so no existing NodeId shifts and the `pumps/` (144 KB) and `robotics/` (691 KB) overlays are untouched.
- Adds **Annex C — Isaac Sim and Omniverse Replicator mapping**.

**Changed — OpenUSD Part 1 (`openusd-binding`)**

- Adds **Annex E — Isaac Sim and Omniverse Replicator mapping** (binding-side view). No information-model change.

> Annex lettering: Part 1 already had A–D after #19 and Part 2 had A–B, so the Isaac Sim annexes land at **E** and **C** respectively.

## Why

A survey of the existing landscape (recorded in full, with quotations and section numbers, in `OPC-UA-Vision-Research.md`) found four gaps that make every vision integration bespoke today:

| Gap | Evidence | What this PR adds |
|---|---|---|
| **Result content is explicitly undefined** | OPC 40100-1 §12.17 and OPC 40001-101 §10.5 both type `ResultContent` as `BaseDataType[]` and say *"application-specific and not defined at this time"*. OPC 40210 §5.1.3 names QIF/DMIS/I++ DMS and then defines *"only the transport"*. | `VisionCharacteristicDataType` shaped on QIF (ISO 23952) Results incl. **measurement uncertainty**, and `VisionDetectionDataType` shaped on ROS 2 `vision_msgs` with 6-DoF poses |
| **No imaging parameters anywhere** | OPC 40100-2 models lenses and lamps in detail, but `VisionImageSensorType` (§9.14) adds **zero members**. No OPC UA spec references GenICam. | `ImageSensorType` with SFNC 2.8 names and PFNC pixel formats |
| **No AI model description** | No released OPC UA AI companion spec; the "OPC UA for AI" WG makes UA consumable *by* AI, not the reverse. 40100-2 has no GPU/NPU typing. | `AiModelType` / `AiDatasetType` / `AiDeploymentType` aligned to IDTA 02060 / 02058 / 02059, plus `InferencePipelineType` and `LearningJobType` |
| **Robot vision does not exist in OPC UA** | OPC 40010-1 v1.02 has **zero** vision, camera, perception, TCP or calibration types; it and OPC 40100 do not reference each other. | ISO 9787 `CoordinateFrameType`, `IntrinsicCalibrationType`, and hand-eye `ExtrinsicCalibrationType` |

**Why it belongs in `metaverse-specs/`.** The organising idea is **sim/real symmetry**: one model describes a physical camera and a simulated one in NVIDIA Isaac Sim identically, so synthetic data generation, training and sim-to-real transfer share a contract with production inspection and robot guidance. That only works if the scene model and the sensor model meet somewhere concrete — and they meet at the **camera prim**, which is why `UsdGeomCameraType` was added to Part 2. Its aperture and focal-length attributes are simultaneously the USD scene description and the imaging intrinsics.

**Media stays out of OPC UA.** Following the GenICam/GigE Vision layering, the model brokers **endpoints** rather than pixels:

- **RTSP/1.0 (RFC 2326) is the mandatory default** streaming protocol and **JPEG the mandatory default** clip format — both are value `0` of their enum, and `validate_local.py` enforces that so the guarantee cannot drift.
- `GetStreamEndpoint` returns a tokenised, expiring lease; `ConfigureStreamEndpoint`, `SelectEndpoint` and `GetClip` complete the API, each with a defined endpoint-selection rule.
- An **optional, size-gated inline facet** lets a client `Read` or **subscribe** to `LatestClip` as a `ByteString`, bounded by `MaxInlineClipSize` ≤ `Server.ServerCapabilities.MaxByteStringLength`, falling back to the URI with `Bad_EncodingLimitsExceeded` on overflow. It is for single stills and the spec says so explicitly — it is not a video path.

**Feedback closes the loop.** `SubmitDetections`, `SubmitInspectionResult`, `SubmitCorrection` and `SubmitImageReference` push bounding boxes and verdicts back into the vision system for overlay, reconciliation, and — most usefully — as corrected ground-truth labels feeding `LearningJobType`.

## Review remediation (commit `a2bb5e3`)

A code review found the first draft **read as design rationale with normative fragments rather than as an implementable specification**: clause 5 contained zero `shall`/`should`/`may`, the 16 Methods had no signatures or StatusCodes anywhere in the document, and Annex A emitted only `NodeId | BrowseName | NodeClass`, so its own claim to carry ModellingRules was false. All 22 findings are addressed.

**Made it a specification** — normative language went from ~3 StatusCode mentions to **49 `shall` and 42 lines citing StatusCodes**:

- New **§6.5, §8.4, §9.4 Method definitions**: every Method now has a signature, per-argument semantics, null/empty handling, preconditions, idempotency rules, and a StatusCode table (`Bad_NotFound`, `Bad_InvalidArgument`, `Bad_InvalidState`, `Bad_ResourceUnavailable`, `Bad_NotSupported`, `Good_Clamped`, …).
- New **§5.10 Units, encodings and conventions**: every physical quantity fixed — including **quaternion order (x, y, z, w)**, the top-left pixel origin, uncertainty at **coverage factor k = 2**, and per-model distortion-coefficient ordering. These previously existed only inside NodeSet `<Description>` elements.
- New **§5.9 ReferenceType definitions**: source/target NodeClass and cardinality, incl. *"an `AiDeploymentType` **shall** have exactly one `UsesModel` reference"* — without which §12.6's `Digest` verification had no path.
- New **§6.6 and §9.5 state transition tables**, with Server-driven vs Method-driven transitions marked.
- **§6.4** gains correlation rules (`LatestClip` and `LatestClipMetadata` in the same NotificationMessage; `Timestamp`+`Digest` as key) and defined initial/disabled states.

**Corrected technical errors:**

- `MaxByteStringLength` is **not** a per-session negotiated value — restated as the `ServerCapabilities` Property plus its interaction with `MaxResponseMessageSize`/`MaxMessageSize`. As written before, the rule was unimplementable.
- **`Cx` sign error** in the intrinsics derivation, in *both* this spec and Scene Annex C — USD's aperture window means a positive offset moves the principal point **left**, so it is a minus.
- Annex C.3 asserted numeric equality across incompatible units; restated as explicit `metersPerUnit` conversions.
- §9.2 named an argument `SubmitCorrection` did not have — the argument was added to the model.

**Model and tooling:** `SubmitCorrection` gains `InlineImage`; `GetStreamEndpoint`/`GetClip` gain an `Endpoint` selector; `StreamEndpointType` gains `ProtocolVersion` (RTSP 2.0 is not backward compatible with 1.0); endpoint folders gain `MandatoryPlaceholder` declarations. Annex A now emits DataType, ValueRank, ModellingRule, structure fields, enum values and full Method signatures — **729 lines, up from 281**.

**Hardened the validator**, which is what caught two real defects the first pass missed:

- It now resolves `UAVariable/@DataType`, asserts enum values are contiguous from 0, and checks overlays for **Mandatory-member presence and DataType conformance**.
- That surfaced: both worked overlays omitted Mandatory members (`InferencePipelineType.Sensor`/`.Deployment`, `ExtrinsicCalibrationType.Transform`/`SourceFrame`/`TargetFrame`, `PerformedAt`, the media Methods), and `RandomizationSeed` was emitted as `String` against a `UInt64` declaration. Both fixed; overlays now also emit real `CoordinateFrameType` frames and a browsable `Vision` root, so they follow the §4.2 discovery path.
- Scene `ClippingRange` now carries `ArrayDimensions="2"`, per Scene §6.2's own normative rule.

## Type

- [ ] Feedback / annotation only (no spec authored — maintainers will draft the change)
- [x] Concrete spec / prose change
- [x] Model change (NodeSet / CSV / generated artifacts, via the tooling)
- [x] Tooling / examples
- [x] Docs

## Checklist

- [x] I edited the **source** (spec document, descriptor, or generator) — not generated NodeSets / CSV / Annex tables by hand
- [x] For a generated-spec change, I regenerated and ran validation (`python core-specs/extras/validate_all.py` and/or the extension's `validate_local.py`)
- [x] I opened this from a topic branch and am ready to discuss

### Validation run

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `python metaverse-specs/validate_all.py --self-contained` | `ALL METAVERSE EXTENSIONS VALIDATED OK` |
| `metaverse-specs/extras/vision/tools/validate_local.py` | `OK - 0 errors` (278 nodes + 254 overlay instance nodes) |
| `python core-specs/extras/validate_all.py --self-contained` | `ALL SELF-CONTAINED EXTENSIONS VALIDATED OK` |
| `npx markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"` | `0 error(s)` across 51 files |
| `.github/scripts/check_links.py` | OK — 753 internal links |
| `.github/scripts/check_yaml_json.py` | OK — 33 JSON, 3 YAML |
| Determinism | Re-running every generator produces **no diff** |

The vision validator additionally enforces two spec invariants that would otherwise be able to drift silently — that `Rtsp` is value 0 and `Jpeg` is value 0 — and I negative-tested both to confirm the check is not a no-op.

### Notes for reviewers

- The research report is committed next to the spec deliberately: `OPC-UA-OpenUSD-Bindings.md` cites a research report that was never committed, so that reference dangles. Committing this one with a relative link means `check_links.py` verifies it.
- The two example overlays are **generated** by `build_examples.py` from a single JSON descriptor each. The existing `openusd-binding` addenda have hand-authored overlay NodeSets with no committed generator, so their prose and XML can drift; this avoids repeating that, and the validator now enforces it.
- Structure-valued members in the overlays (`Transform`, `Intrinsics`) are declared with the correct DataType but carry no encoded `Value`; the concrete numbers are tabulated in the addenda instead. Encoding nested structure values in NodeSet XML is error-prone and adds little for a worked example — happy to change this if reviewers prefer.
- NodeIds throughout are **provisional**, per repo convention.

### Open questions the working group may want to settle

1. Should `VisionCharacteristicDataType` carry a QIF `QPId` so a result can be *joined* to a QIF document rather than only being structurally convertible?
2. Should the media-endpoint model be factored out for reuse by any OPC UA spec that needs to broker a stream, rather than living in a vision spec?
3. When the AAS V3 companion spec lands, should the AI types reference it directly instead of aligning only by field name?
4. Is `Bad_EncodingLimitsExceeded` the right StatusCode for an oversized inline clip, or should a Vision-specific code be defined?


## Worked examples promoted to Annex F and Annex G (commit `a7c9198`)

The robotics and machine-vision worked examples existed only as separate documents beside their overlays, so a reader of `OPC-UA-Vision.md` never saw a worked instance of the model it defines. Both are now annexes of the specification, spliced in as generated content between `<!-- BEGIN GENERATED -->` markers — the same mechanism the `arrow-encoding` and `avro-encoding` generators use, not a copy.

One renderer emits both forms from the single descriptor: standalone with level-2 sections and links relative to `vision/<folder>/`, or annex with sections demoted and renumbered `F.n` / `G.n` and links rebased to `vision/`. Neither form can drift from the other or from the overlay, and the repository determinism check now covers the annex text. The validator additionally checks both marker pairs are present and that each region still contains its annex heading — without which the splice would silently stop updating and the spec would keep a stale example while everything else regenerated.

Annexes were **appended** as F and G rather than inserted, so the cross-references to Annexes C, D and E stay valid.

## Review feedback addressed (commit `0328900`)

Three review threads on `OPC-UA-Vision.md`, all resolved.

**Clause 5 was an enumeration of types with no explanation of why they exist or when they are used.** It now opens with a five-group map of the 25 ObjectTypes keyed to the question each group answers, plus **two new diagrams**: a type hierarchy showing the four abstract bases and the interface, and an instance-structure diagram showing every type with its members and its hierarchical, ReferenceType and NodeId-Property relationships — distinguishing the three kinds of edge. Below them, the three chains a client actually traverses are spelled out: imagery, meaning of a pose, and provenance of an answer (the chain that explains why `UsesModel` has cardinality exactly 1).

Each subclause from the sensor types onward now states **why it exists**, **when a Server instantiates it**, and **what a client does with it** — including why `VisionSensorType` is an abstract base and `IVisionSimulatedType` an interface rather than subtypes, and why the DataTypes are structures rather than folders of Variables.

> This inserted two subclauses, so §5.1–§5.10 shifted to §5.3–§5.12. Every cross-reference in the spec, the generators and the validator's error messages was remapped and verified against the actual headings.

**AI models are business artefacts, not device firmware.** New **§8.1.1** states this as the assumption the AI clause rests on, with three normative consequences: model and device lifecycles are independent (a model change `shall not` require a firmware change, and `AiModelType.Version` `shall not` be tied to a device version); the Server *describes* what is deployed and its provenance while approval and release governance stay with the operator's own system, reached through `ProvenanceUri`; and authority to change a model is separate from authority to operate the device (§12.5). The vendor-supplied fixed-model case remains expressible, but as one case rather than the assumption.

**Clause 1.3 is now "What this specification does not (yet) do"**, separating the two permanent boundaries (no pixels on the default path; not replacing GenICam et al.) from the two deferrals (no recipe format; no normative dependency on OPC 40100 / 40010 / DI / Machinery / OpenUSD), so a reader can tell a scope decision from an omission.

Also corrected a leftover in the §5.11 table, which still named the `UsesModel` InverseName as `IsUsedByPipeline` after the model was changed to `IsUsedByDeployment`.

**Verified:** 52 Mermaid diagrams compile including both new ones, markdownlint 0 errors, 767 links OK, both `validate_all` suites OK, vision validator 0 errors, generators byte-deterministic.


## Security review — 9 findings fixed (commit `c1195dd`)

A `/security-review` pass produced 9 findings. **Seven were in the specification itself**, not the code — flaws that would have propagated to every implementer. All are fixed and each fix was negative-tested.

| Severity | Finding | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **HIGH** | `PromoteModel` privilege escalation — §12.5 said *should* require distinct authorization while §8.1.1 and §9.4 asserted it as required, so resolving in favour of the defining clause let any feedback-authorized principal promote a model to **every** deployment fed by the job | §12.5 now `shall`, explicitly not implied by feedback or collection authorization; condition added to *VIS-Learning* so it is testable |
| **HIGH** | **SSRF** — §12.3 assumed all URIs were server-provided, but `VisionImageReferenceDataType.Uri` also arrives via `SubmitImageReference` (required by *VIS-Feedback*), and §9.3 requires the Server to dereference and retain it | §12.3 split by direction; inbound half requires a scheme allowlist, rejection of loopback/link-local/unique-local, **re-validation after DNS and after every redirect**, response bounds, digest-before-admission, and no failure-detail disclosure |
| MEDIUM | Digest integrity unenforceable — `DigestAlgorithm` accepted any IANA name incl. `md5`/`sha-1`, and `Digest` was Optional with a *should* | Both now **Mandatory**; ≥256-bit with no known collision weakness; MD5/SHA-1 banned; clients must refuse unknown algorithms rather than skip verification |
| MEDIUM | Credential-bearing media URIs had no confidentiality requirement, and `MediaEndpointType.SecureTransport` appeared **zero times** in the document | `SecureTransport` made Mandatory and given normative meaning; credentials only over `SignAndEncrypt` + confidential transport, else `Bad_SecurityModeInsufficient`; never written to a log |
| MEDIUM | `ResultId` is Server-global but was unscoped on per-sensor/per-pipeline Methods, bypassing §12.1 authorization | Scoped to the owning object without disclosing existence elsewhere; unpredictability required |
| MEDIUM | No clause on feedback *content* integrity — client labels flow to `CandidateModel` unattributed | New **§12.7**: caller identity per retained sample, client samples distinguishable in the dataset, distinct gate before training, overlays visually distinguishable with bounded TTL |
| MEDIUM | Robotics example advertised plaintext `grpc://` while the adjacent text claimed a §12.6 authenticated channel | Corrected to `grpcs://`; `SecureTransport` in overlays is now **derived from the endpoint scheme**, so an example cannot claim protection its own URI contradicts |
| LOW | `build_examples.py` built paths from unvalidated descriptor fields | `outputFolder`/`domain` pattern-checked; resolved directory asserted to stay under `vision/` |
| LOW | XML injection — attributes used `sx.escape` (which does not escape quotes) and `exampleNamespaceUri` was unescaped entirely | `sx.quoteattr` for attributes, `sx.escape` for the URI |

The XML fix was verified by injecting a BrowseName that closes its own attribute plus a namespace URI carrying a whole `<UAObject>`: both come out inert, no node is injected, and the document still parses. The validator also caught the newly-Mandatory members missing from both worked overlays — which is exactly the "spec changed, model didn't" class of half-fix earlier review rounds kept surfacing.

## Data Channels as an optional media transport (commits `9722981`, `af02a97`)

Merged `main` (which now carries **OPC UA — Data Channels**, PR #22) and added it as **one more option** for streaming media — never an obligation.

That draft's `HasDataChannel` description names **a camera** as its first motivating case, and `IDataChannelSourceType` states that adding the interface is *"the only change a companion specification needs in order to become streamable."* Vision brokers media out-of-band precisely because OPC UA had no streaming primitive, so this is genuinely new: media on the SecureChannel the client **already has** — no second protocol, no second port, no media credential.

**It is optional, and the spec is built so it stays that way:**

- *VIS-Base* still requires *VIS-Media-Rtsp* and *VIS-Media-Jpeg*; §6.2's "assume without negotiation" guarantee is unchanged **word for word**.
- New **`VIS-Media-DataChannel`** facet is optional and marked in its own row as depending on a draft.
- §6.3 **forbids** selecting a data-channel endpoint unless the caller explicitly passed `PreferredProtocol = DataChannel` — a client that cannot open one is never handed an endpoint it cannot use.
- §6.7 spells out graceful absence: absent `DataChannelCapabilities` ⇒ unsupported; `Bad_ServiceUnsupported` is definitive; clients **shall not** probe with frames; the §6.2 out-of-band path is always the fallback.

**Draft status is stated three times** — clause 2 (informative, explicitly non-normative), a callout at the head of §6.7, and the facet row.

**No dependency is taken, and that is enforced.** Data Channels is a *base-namespace* errata using **provisional `65000+` NodeIds**, so a type-level `HasInterface` to `IDataChannelSourceType` would dangle and **fail NodeSet load** on every Server that has not adopted it. The binding is therefore prose plus two appended Optional members on the shared `MediaEndpointType` base — `DataChannelSource` (NodeId) and `DataChannelContentType` (String), inherited by stream *and* clip endpoints — plus `VisionStreamProtocolEnum.DataChannel = 8`. Appended, so **nothing moved**: the CSV gained exactly `6196` and `6197`. If the draft is withdrawn the members go permanently null and nothing else changes.

**Clips are covered too.** Where both facets exist a Server *should* offer an oversized still on the data channel rather than only returning `Bad_EncodingLimitsExceeded`, since a data channel has no `MaxByteStringLength` ceiling. *VIS-Media-Inline* is explicitly **not** deprecated — it is the only in-band still path for a Server without the draft. Correlation reuses the existing §6.4 rule 4 `Timestamp` + `Digest` mechanism rather than inventing a second one.

**Security bonus:** a data channel inherits the SecureChannel's security, so it needs **no media credential at all** — sidestepping the §12.2 credential-exposure requirements entirely. Two conditions added: `SecureTransport` true only on a `SignAndEncrypt` channel, and media **shall not** rely on `AllowInsecureDataChannels`.

The robotics example demonstrates the *additional-path* case on both endpoints, with plain `BaseObjectType` stand-ins for the Server-created sources and prose explaining why the overlay emits no provisional ids.

**Four new validator checks, each negative-tested** — the `DataChannel` literal exists and is the highest (proving it was appended); `MediaEndpointType` carries both members; an overlay claiming `StreamProtocol = DataChannel` also carries `DataChannelSource`; and the load-bearing one: the Vision NodeSet references **no** id in `65000–65999`. That check caught an injected `i=65010` immediately, so the no-dependency property is mechanically enforced rather than merely intended.

### Final validation

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `metaverse-specs/validate_all.py --self-contained` | `ALL METAVERSE EXTENSIONS VALIDATED OK` |
| `extras/vision/tools/validate_local.py` | `OK - 0 errors` (280 nodes + 284 overlay nodes) |
| `core-specs/extras/validate_all.py --self-contained` | `ALL SELF-CONTAINED EXTENSIONS VALIDATED OK` |
| `npx markdownlint-cli2 "**/*.md"` | `0 error(s)` |
| `check_links.py` / `check_yaml_json.py` | OK — 872 links; 33 JSON, 3 YAML |
| `check_mermaid.py` | OK — 55 diagrams compiled |
| Determinism | Re-running every generator produces no diff |


## Review round 3 — 18 threads addressed (commit `a8056cc`)

**Prose structure.** Removed *every* bold rubric — `**Why it exists.**`, `**When a Server instantiates it.**`, `**What a client does with it.**`, plus `**Why structures rather than folders**`, `**Why the enumerations are closed**`, `**Why references rather than only Properties**`, `**Design note**`, `**What it is for**` and `**What this specification does not define**`. Each is now running prose that states the reason directly rather than contrasting it with what the design could also have been ("This type exists because…", "A Server instantiates it…", "A client uses it to…").

**§5.10 and §5.11 expanded.** §5.10 had two bare comma-separated lists — seventeen enumeration names and nine structure names with no indication of purpose; both are now tables with a one-line explanation and a cross-reference for each. §5.11 had a five-row table and nothing else; each ReferenceType now has a paragraph explaining what following it in *each direction* answers.

**Terminology.** Clause 3 gains **point cloud**, **6-DoF pose**, **frame** (with an explicit warning that it is not a video frame), **intrinsic** / **extrinsic** / **hand-eye calibration**, **ground truth**, **inference** and **facet**. *Sim/real symmetry* is now explained at §4.3 where it is first used, not only in the glossary.

**Usage models with sequence diagrams.** New **§8.2.1** documents each `InferenceLocation` option with a table and four sequence diagrams — the first showing that the client's exchange is *identical* in all four cases (the point of the property), the rest showing that only the failure modes differ. New **§9.1** explains why a return path is needed at all, defines "return path" in the control-loop sense, and adds a sequence diagram covering all three feedback purposes. Both state machines (§6.6, §9.6) gain `stateDiagram-v2` diagrams above their transition tables.

**New Annex H — GenICam binding.** Replaces the scattered "borrowing the names is deliberate" sentences with a real binding: all fourteen `ImageSensorType` members against SFNC 2.8 with conversions, the **selector** and **`…Auto`** conventions that trip implementers, PFNC families, device identity, and an explicit list of what deliberately has *no* binding.

**ONVIF.** The research report had no coverage despite ONVIF being dominant in network video. New **§3.1a** compares Profiles S, T and M, notes ONVIF reached the same endpoint-brokering layering independently, identifies **Profile M as the strongest external evidence that result content can be standardised**, and gives four concrete reasons it is not usable here (surveillance vocabulary, no ISO 14253 uncertainty, no 6-DoF pose in a named frame, no model description). **Annex E.2** carries the mapping.

Plus: OPC 40010-1 named explicitly in §1.1, `no members at all` unbolded, "on a" → "over" in §6.7, "by the business" → "by the end-user" in §8.1.1.

Clause 9 and Annex E subclauses renumbered as a result; every cross-reference remapped and verified. `check_mermaid` now compiles **62 diagrams**, up from 55 — all seven new ones render.


## Branch brought current with `main` (commits `e3c8753`, `ad55438`, `84f2a70`, `f638a65`)

Four merges from `main`, covering the OpenUSD 0.4.0 / xRegistry rework, the point-in-time voice rewrite of both OpenUSD specs, the landing READMEs, the submittable xRegistry domain spec, the Avro/Arrow consolidation, and two Data Channels changes (certificate rotation, serialized STR securing). One conflict arose in each of the first two merges; both were the same additive shape and both sides were kept:

- **`extras/openusd-scene/tools/build_model.py`** — `main` appended `UsdAttributeType.ConnectionPaths`, this branch appended `UsdGeomCameraType` and its ten members. Member NodeIds in that generator are positional, so ordering decides them: `ConnectionPaths` is declared **first** because it is already published on `main` at `6078` and must keep that id, and the camera members absorbed the shift to `6079–6088`. Verified mechanically — every row in main's `NodeIds.csv` is byte-identical after the merge.
- **`metaverse-specs/validate_all.py`** — both sides registered a validator (`openusd-artifacts` ×2 from `main`, `vision` from this branch). All kept.

The generated NodeSet, CSV and Annex artifacts that conflicted were resolved by **regenerating from the merged source** rather than hand-merging, per the repository convention.

Because `main` rewrote both OpenUSD specs into point-in-time voice and *wrote that style down* in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, a clean textual merge could silently reintroduce the voice the rewrite removed. Checked: the lines this branch adds to either OpenUSD spec contain no version references or historical phrasing, and the Vision spec's `Release 0.1.0` mentions are scope and identity statements, which the guide explicitly permits.

Likewise, the two Data Channels commits mattered here even without a textual conflict, since §6.7 and §12 are written against that draft. Every identifier this branch cites still resolves on `main` — `DataChannelCapabilities`, `OpenDataChannel`, `Bad_ServiceUnsupported`, `IDataChannelSourceType`, `DataChannelSourceType`, `HasDataChannel`, `AllowInsecureDataChannels`, `ContentType`, and the *Data Channel Media Server Facet* — and the provisional NodeId block is still `65000+`.

## Validator hardening (commit `0a6b5d5`)

The guard that keeps §6.7 a prose-only binding rejected references in `65000–65999`, but the Data Channels draft allocates `65000..65099` types, `65100..65199` well-known instances, `65900..65999` EnumStrings and **`66000+` members** — so a reference to a member declaration fell straight through the check whose entire purpose is to catch it. Range widened to `66999` and negative-tested with `i=66001`, which the old guard accepted and the new one rejects. Pre-existing gap, surfaced while verifying the merge.

items.title: unified-bench: label WAL-excluded durable storage
items.body:
## Objective

Close the remaining #1954 report/accounting gap by making column-store benchmark storage labels explicitly WAL-excluded for steady-state comparisons, while preserving the literal WAL segment filename grammar in generated Markdown output and tightening the exclusion filter to match valid command WAL segments only.

## Context

#1955 needs honest storage labels before final JSONBench parity reporting. This PR keeps #1954 scoped to report-only durable storage accounting: WAL bytes are diagnostic, while value-log/leaf-log bytes remain durable storage.

Corrected 100k external context retained for reporting wording only:

- shape/layout/owner: `full-retained-json`, `column-store-full-prepared`, `typed_column_part`
- reconstruction: valid
- total: 70,726,513 bytes
- typed-column part: 11,966,546 bytes
- column asset: 13,667,330 bytes
- primary index: 4,194,304 bytes
- WAL: 49,639,046 bytes

## Non-goals

- No destructive GC/rewrite/cleanup behavior changes.
- No WAL truncation or checkpoint semantics changes.
- No on-disk format changes.
- No codec/compression/layout optimization; #1952 remains the storage-compression lane.
- No prepared mutation-query enablement; mutation-bearing prepared physical queries remain fail-closed.
- No #730 or #1943 work.

## Design

- Adds `durable_storage_bytes_wal_excluded` to `cmd/unified_bench` column-store byte accounting.
- Adds `wal_bytes_excluded_from_durable_storage` as the diagnostic subtraction input.
- Excludes only valid command WAL segment files named `wal/commit-l<lane>-<seq>.log` (numeric lane, non-zero sequence).
- Requires WAL-excluded bytes to come from regular files only, so directories, recovery artifacts, and non-segment files are not counted as WAL bytes.
- Rejects non-digit lane/sequence tokens before parsing, so names such as `commit-lane-readme.log`, `commit-l+1-000001.log`, or seq=0 segments are intentionally not excluded.
- Keeps durable `ordinary_value_vlog_bytes`, `leaf_vlog_bytes`, `primary_index_bytes`, column assets, and manifest/control bytes included in the WAL-excluded durable label.
- Keeps manifest/control bytes separate from referenced column asset bytes.
- Keeps `command_wal_bytes_before_checkpoint` as before-checkpoint diagnostic evidence and aligned to valid command WAL segment files only.
- Ensures Markdown report text preserves the literal grammar by rendering the segment pattern as code span: `` `wal/commit-l<lane>-<seq>.log` ``.
- Removes the machine-local `/tmp/...` artifact path from checked-in lifecycle docs while preserving the corrected 100k reporting figures and context wording.

## Scope

- Includes (files/symbols):
  - `cmd/unified_bench/suite_column_store.go`
  - `cmd/unified_bench/suite_column_store_test.go`
  - `cmd/unified_bench/README.md`
  - `TreeDB/docs/spec/typed-column-lifecycle-1954.md`
  - `columnStoreSuiteCommandWALLogBytes`
  - `columnStoreSuiteCommandWALLogName`
  - `columnStoreSuiteDecimalDigits`
  - `columnStoreDurableStorageWALExcludedNote`

**Add a new subsection in §2 (or wherever the cross-library probe matrix lives) titled `Identity-map ORMs do not solve cyclic serialization`.** Content (paraphrase, do not copy verbatim — the agent should write this in the doc's existing voice):

> A common assumption is that ORMs with built-in identity maps (Hibernate's Persistence Context, EF Core's ChangeTracker, SQLAlchemy's Session, MikroORM's IdentityMap) "solve" the cyclic graph problem — that is, they produce a fully populated cyclic in-memory object graph that downstream consumers can use freely.
>
> The supporting-probes evidence in `reference/v1/` confirms half of this is true: identity-map ORMs do produce a single live instance per database row, validated by the smartCheck assertion (one logical id → one runtime object, even when traversed via a cyclic relationship). All four identity-map ORMs tested — SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, EF Core, and MikroORM — pass the hydration check.
>
> But none of them solve the *consumer* problem. > The pattern is universal: identity-map hydration is necessary but not sufficient. Without an explicit cycle-aware serialization step (Two-Pass Wire's flat-form approach, or a library-specific reference handler), every identity-map ORM crashes the moment a downstream consumer tries to materialize the cyclic graph as a tree-shaped output. ```nb-meta

```nb-meta
slug: constrained-decoding
mode: open
template: article

title: A grammar masks all but seven of GPT-2's 50,257 tokens to force valid output
order: null
```

## Task

<details><summary>Full artifact</summary>

````text
# Commission — The Build

## Subject and angle
**How constrained decoding forces a language model to emit guaranteed-valid
structured output.** The mechanism, built up from the sampling loop: at each
step the model produces a probability distribution over the vocabulary; a
grammar or finite-state machine tracks which tokens could legally come next
given what has been generated so far; the illegal tokens' logits are masked to
`-inf` before the softmax, so the model can only sample a token that keeps the
output valid. Teach it the way Simon Willison would — run the thing, show the
receipts — with Dan Luu's insistence on measuring the cost, not just asserting
it, and Julia Evans's refusal to wave anything away as obvious.

The article must contain **real, runnable code in `rs-code` blocks**: a minimal
constrained sampler a practitioner could paste and run (a small regex/JSON
grammar → an FSM/index → per-step logit mask over a real tokenizer). Show what
the mask does to the distribution on a concrete step. Then be honest about the
tradeoffs the naïve version hides: the cost of building the token-level index,
the tokenizer-alignment problem (grammar symbols are characters, the model
speaks tokens), and where constrained decoding changes *what* the model says,
not just its shape (the "structure can hurt quality" critique). A performance
number arrives with its baseline.

## Mode / duty
`open` section (Engineering), template `article`. Duty 2026-07-17 assigned
the-build as an open section: invent tonight's topic within the beat. This is
that topic. Words: **1500–2800**.

## Catalog — do not repeat
Only one the-build article is published: `speculative-decoding` ("A small draft
model makes Chinchilla 70B decode 2.5× faster"). That piece already owns the
*sampling/decoding-speed* framing at the token level. Keep this piece on
**validity and structure**, not throughput; if you touch speed, it is the
overhead constrained decoding *adds*, framed against speculative decoding only
as a contrast if useful. Do not re-teach how sampling works from zero at
speculative-decoding's length; assume that reader.

## Publishing tonight (avoid collisions)
Six articles run tonight. Adjacent ones: **the-paper** covers the *Muon
optimizer* and **the-wire** is the AI daily brief for 2026-07-17. Keep this an
evergreen engineering explainer — do not chase a same-day news peg that the
wire would own, and do not drift into optimizer/training territory.

## Known-good starting sources (verify; researcher will expand)
- Brandon T. Willard & Rémi Louf, "Efficient Guided Generation for Large
  Language Models" (Outlines paper, arXiv 2307.09702) — the FSM-index method.
  PRIMARY for the algorithm.
- `outlines` library source (dottxt-ai/outlines) — the implementation.
- llama.cpp GBNF grammar docs (`grammars/README.md`) — grammar-constrained
  sampling in a production engine. PRIMARY for that approach.
- OpenAI "Structured Outputs" docs and its engineering write-up — a hosted
  implementation and its stated guarantees/limits.
- Independent critique of quality/latency costs (e.g. analyses of
  "does JSON mode hurt reasoning"). Bring a real measurement.

## Source policy (floor — proof enforces)
`min_sources: 8`. Series is **not** `strict`. No kind bands, but the house
Citations rule still holds: prefer primaries (the papers, the library source,
the engine docs) and cite only what you read.

## Output
`library/the-build/constrained-decoding.html`

## Provenance for nb-meta (you know the runtime; the roles do not)
- `harness`: `claude-code-routine`
- `model`: `claude-opus-4-8`
- `mode`: `open`  ·  `template`: `article`  ·  `date`: `2026-07-17`

## The one thing this piece must do
Leave a practitioner able to *build* a constrained decoder and to *judge when
to reach for one* — including when its guarantee of valid shape costs them
something in the content. Not a tour of libraries: the mechanism, in code, with
its costs measured.

---
### PR-body flag (include verbatim in the PR body — PROTOCOL §Runtime)
````

````text
# Editor's report — the-build/constrained-decoding

## VERDICT

**NEEDS WRITER CHANGES (minor).** The piece is substantively sound: the
mechanism is built in runnable code, the mask's effect is shown on a concrete
step with a reproducible receipt, all three costs carry a measured number with
its baseline, every load-bearing claim traces to the research log, and there
are no fabricated or off-roster sources. The proof is at **BLOCK: 0**. This is
**not a redraft** and **not a researcher sourcing pass**. What remains is a
short list of writer touch-ups (one floor violation in the lede, a heading
cadence that collides with the neighbor piece, one quote-fidelity nit) plus one
factual error I corrected in place and one advisory verification the desk should
run before publish.

Routing: **writer**, light. No researcher action required.

- Unresolved objections (writer/researcher): **3**
- Advisory (desk): **1**
- Fixed by editor this pass: **2** (state-count error corrected; two cut lines)

---

## Read 1 — Skeptic

`Skeptic: thesis "constrained decoding guarantees valid structure by masking every illegal token's logit to -inf per step; you can build one from the grammar up, and it carries three measurable costs — index build, tokenizer alignment, and a content change that is conditional on schema/prompt design"; tested 7 claims; broke: none load-bearing.`

Every figure checked against the log and reconciled:

- **O(N) naive / O(1)-average masking, index memory ~= FSM states** — Willard &
  Louf quotes are verbatim against research source 1. Good.
- **Index build ~3.5 s Outlines vs ~0 ms Guidance** — traces to JSONSchemaBench
  (source 8); baseline present. Good.
- **Alignment tax: 1,134 of 128k tokens (<1%) context-dependent** — XGrammar
  (source 2); baseline (128k vocab) present. Good.
- **Per-step mask <40 us, up to 100x vs Outlines v1.0 / llama.cpp; TPOT 6.2->6.3 ms
  (batch 1), 9.0->9.1 (batch 16)** — XGrammar; framed correctly as the overhead
  constrained decoding *adds* against unconstrained generation, which is the one
  speed framing the commission permits. The 80x end-to-end throughput number
  from the same paper is (correctly) left out. Good.
- **Quality: GSM8K 75.99 -> 49.25, LLaMA-3-8B last-letter 70.07 -> 28.00 (harm,
  Tam); 0.77 -> 0.78 (dottxt) and 83.8 vs 80.1 (JSONSchemaBench, no-harm)** — all
  verbatim/located against sources 6, 7, 8, and the harm case is never stated in
  isolation. The steelman/rebuttal/resolution structure matches the log's
  Contradictions section. Good.
- **Hard-schema coverage 3-41%** — JSONSchemaBench Table 4; used as the honesty
  check on "guaranteed valid." Good.
- **The receipt (Fig. 7)** — I recomputed the softmax by hand from the stated
  logits: 0.4908 -> 0.0000 (` maybe`), 0.3636 -> 0.8527 (`true`), 0.0601 -> 0.1410
  (`false`) all reproduce exactly, and the arithmetic only closes if exactly
  seven tokens are legal. Internally consistent.

Sourcing honesty is a strength. The gated OpenAI announcement blog (log source
5) is *not* cited, and the two claims that depended on it — the CFG-over-FSM
mechanism and the "100%" reliability figure — are absent. The dottxt rebuttal is
labeled `primary` with an inline note disclosing it is "a party with a stake,"
matching the log's independence caveat, and JSONSchemaBench is correctly framed
as the neutral referee. No kind is mislabeled; no citation runs past the roster.

**One broken factual claim (fixed in place, not writer-facing):** the prose said
the `true | false` DFA has **"Nine states"** (and "nine-state boolean"). The code
that owns the claim, Fig. 1's `DELTA`, uses states 0-9 — **ten** states
(true-branch 0->1->3->4->5, false-branch 0->2->6->7->8->9). There are nine
*transitions*, ten states. The primary (the code) governs, so I corrected the
prose to "Ten states" / "ten-state boolean" in both places.

## Read 2 — Cut

`Cut: 2 sentences; worst tell: "The interesting part is how narrow the mask really is." — the piece grading its own material.`

Two sentences failed the delete test and are gone:

1. Orientation: *"The interesting part is how narrow the mask really is."* — the
   piece telling the reader what is interesting instead of showing it. The
   demonstration that follows ("Compile a grammar... exactly seven tokens
   survive") carries the point without the label.
2. Alignment section: *"The expensive one percent is what the naive index
   quietly leaves on the table."* — a manufactured punchline restating the
   sentence directly above it (the 1,134 tokens "have to be rechecked as
   generation proceeds"); "leaves on the table" is idiom standing in for a fact
   already delivered.

## Read 3 — Reader

`Reader: this gives me a from-scratch DFA -> per-state token index -> logit mask over the real 50,257-token GPT-2 vocabulary, a printed step showing the model's favorite token (` maybe`, p=0.49) deleted while `true` climbs 0.36 -> 0.85, and a reconciliation of the contested "structure hurts reasoning" evidence into a rule (harm tracks schema placement and prompt, not the mask).`

This is genuine original work, not a restatement of the sources — it matches the
writer's sentence in research.md § Original work, and the draft shows the work
(Figs. 2, 3, 6, 7) rather than claiming it. Not a redraft.

**Voice:** closer to the exemplars than to a median AI summary. The command ->
receipt rhythm is Willison; every cost arrives measured against a baseline in
Luu's register; the tokenizer joint is opened with the plain, almost-childlike
Evans question ("So which states does a single token move the machine through,
and how does the index know?"). The two tells I cut were the main pull toward
the median.

**Headline** survives as the largest claim: the piece establishes exactly "all
but seven of GPT-2's 50,257 tokens" at Fig. 3. **Dek** makes a claim about the
world (FSM marks legal tokens; rival logits -> -inf before sampling), adds the
mechanism the headline withholds, and does not restate it or fall into a banned
mold. Both pass.

**No source asset requested.** The article's own logit printout (Fig. 7) is the
right visual evidence, exactly as the log recommended; the XGrammar figure it
held in reserve would be redundant.
````

````text
# Research: the-build/constrained-decoding

The mechanism is well-sourced and the code the writer must build rests on a
primary that gives the actual algorithms. Willard & Louf (Outlines, arXiv
2307.09702) own the method: reduce generation to walking a finite-state
machine, precompute a map from FSM state to the subset of the vocabulary that
keeps the output valid, and at each step mask every other token's logit before
the softmax. Their complexity claim is the spine of the "costs" argument —
per-step masking is O(1) average against a naive O(N) loop over the whole
vocabulary, but that speed is *bought* with a one-time index built over the
vocabulary, and building it is where the bill lands (Outlines ~3.5 s grammar
compilation in JSONSchemaBench vs Guidance ~0 ms; OpenAI's first-request
latency). The tokenizer-alignment problem is real and named in the primary:
the grammar counts characters, the model emits subword tokens, so a single
token can traverse several FSM states, and the index must record every
sub-path a token string can match (Outlines Algorithm 3; XGrammar's
"context-dependent tokens," <1% of a 128k vocab but the expensive 1%). The
performance-number-with-baseline is strongest from XGrammar (up to 100x lower
per-token masking latency, <40 µs, near-zero TPOT overhead vs unconstrained)
and from the Outlines O(1)-vs-O(N) claim. The "structure hurts quality"
critique is genuinely contested and that is the log's most valuable seam: "Let
Me Speak Freely?" measured large reasoning drops under JSON constraints
(GSM8K 75.99% → 49.25% on GPT-3.5-turbo), but two independent re-runs holding
the prompt fixed (dottxt's rebuttal; JSONSchemaBench) found constrained
decoding *matches or beats* free-form — so the degradation tracks prompt and
parsing choices, not the mask itself. Thin spots: I could not read the OpenAI
announcement blog directly (403 to fetchers), so its CFG-over-FSM mechanism and
its "100%" reliability figure are logged as claimed-not-verified; and I did not
recover the exact numbers behind the Outlines paper's Guidance benchmark
figure, only its verified qualitative claim.

## Contradictions

- **Does constrained decoding hurt reasoning?** Sharpest disagreement in the
  log, and the piece's honest center.
  - FOR harm: source 6 (Tam et al.) — GSM8K 75.99% → 49.25%, Last Letter drops
    up to ~42 pt under JSON-mode; concludes reasoning "significantly declines."
  - AGAINST: source 7 (dottxt, a party) re-ran with matched prompts and found
    structured ≥ unstructured (GSM8K 0.77 → 0.78); source 8 (JSONSchemaBench,
    independent) found constrained decoding "achieves higher performance than
    the unconstrained setting" (+3.7 pt on GSM8K).
  - Resolution the evidence supports: the measured degradation in source 6
    tracks (a) mismatched/under-specified prompts, (b) conflating OpenAI's
    non-masked "JSON mode" with true grammar-constrained decoding, and (c)
    placing the answer where the model cannot reason into it first — NOT the
    logit mask per se. The mask constrains *shape*; it changes *content* only
    when the allowed-token set at a step excludes what the model would have said
    to reason well (e.g. forcing an answer field before a rationale field). The
    writer should state the harm is real but conditional, and name the
    conditions, rather than either "structure is free" or "structure hurts."
- **"Guaranteed valid" vs measured coverage.** OpenAI (source 4) and Outlines
  (source 1) frame output as guaranteed schema-valid. JSONSchemaBench (source 8,
  Table 4) shows real engines drop to 3–41% coverage on hard schemas (timeouts,
  unsupported schema features; cf. OpenAI's own "some features are
  unavailable"). The guarantee is "valid per the grammar the engine actually
  compiled," which for hard schemas may be a reduced grammar or may time out —
  not "valid per your full JSON Schema in all cases." Worth a sentence of
  honesty.
- **Where the mask meets the tokenizer.** Source 1 treats subword alignment as
  solved by Algorithm 3 (enumerate FSM sub-paths a token accepts). Source 2
  (XGrammar) shows it is not free: ~1% of a 128k vocab are "context-dependent"
  tokens that must be re-checked at runtime, and that 1% is the part the naive
  precomputed index cannot fully absorb. No contradiction on facts, but a
  tension in emphasis the "slow down at the joint" move should surface.

## Numbers

Every load-bearing figure, its owner, and what one unit counts:

- **O(1) average per-step masking vs O(N) naive** — source 1, Section 3. N =
  vocabulary size. "O(1)" counts hash-map lookups per generated token after the
  index exists; "O(N)" counts a scan over all N tokens per step without it.
- **<40 µs per-token mask; up to 100x reduction vs Outlines v1.0 / llama.cpp
  b3998** — source 2, Section 4.1 / Fig. 9. Unit: microseconds of masking work
  per generated token. Baseline: the two named prior engines.
- **TPOT ~unchanged: 6.2 ms (off) → 6.3 ms (on), batch 1; 9.0 → 9.1 ms, batch
  16** — source 2, Table 1. Unit: milliseconds per output token. Baseline:
  unconstrained generation, same model/hardware. This is the cleanest
  "cost measured against baseline" number in the log.
- **80x end-to-end serving speedup vs vLLM+Outlines / llama.cpp** — source 2,
  Abstract, H100. Unit: end-to-end structured-output serving throughput/latency.
  (Use as engine-level context, not as the article's core claim — commission
  keeps throughput off-center.)
- **Context-dependent tokens: 1,134 of 128k (<1%), reducible to 120 (−90%)** —
  source 2, Sections 3.1–3.2. Unit: vocabulary tokens needing runtime grammar
  re-check. This is the quantified size of the tokenizer-alignment tax.
- **Index/grammar build cost: Outlines ~3.5 s compilation (vs Guidance ~0 ms)** —
  source 8, Table 2. Unit: one-time seconds to compile a schema into the token
  index. Corroborated qualitatively by source 4 (OpenAI first-request latency;
  a secondary put standard schemas at "<10 s," complex "up to a minute" — treat
  the minute figure as secondary/unverified).
- **Reasoning under JSON-mode (harm case): GSM8K 75.99% → 49.25%; Last Letter
  56.74% → 25.20% (GPT-3.5-turbo), 70.07% → 28.00% (LLaMA-3-8B)** — source 6.
  Unit: task accuracy %. Baseline: same model, natural-language free-form.
- **Reasoning under constraint (no-harm case): GSM8K 0.77 → 0.78 (source 7);
  Guidance 83.8% vs LM-only 80.1%, +3.7 pt (source 8, Table 8)** — Unit: task
  accuracy. Baseline: unconstrained, matched prompt. Report alongside the harm
  case; never in isolation.
- **TPOT can drop below unconstrained: Guidance 6.37 ms vs LM-only 15.40 ms** —
  source 8, Table 2. Unit: ms/token. Mechanism: jump-forward/skipping
  grammar-forced deterministic tokens. Use carefully — it is one engine on one
  dataset, and it brushes the throughput framing the commission fences off.
- **OpenAI reliability "100%"** — source 5, GATED. Log as "OpenAI states,"
  not verified. Do NOT publish the "<40% without" figure; unverifiable from what
  I read.

## Source assets

- **XGrammar Fig. 9** (per-token latency bars, source 2): shows the 100x /
  <40 µs gap against Outlines and llama.cpp. A crop must keep the axis units
  (µs, log scale if present), the engine labels, and the XGrammar bar; it must
  drop any unrelated panels. Strong candidate if the writer wants one measured
  chart — but the piece can instead render its OWN mask/logit printout, which
  the voice brief explicitly prefers ("paste the receipt"). Prefer the writer's
  own output; hold Fig. 9 as backup.
- **XGrammar Table 1** (TPOT off vs on): the cleanest baseline-relative number;
  better rendered by the writer as a tiny two-row `data-nb-chart` or inline than
  lifted as an image.
- **"Let Me Speak Freely?" results table** (source 6) and **JSONSchemaBench
  Table 8** (source 8): the two sides of the quality debate. If the writer
  builds a comparison chart, it should place the harm-case and the
  matched-prompt no-harm case side by side with the prompt-condition labeled —
  the honest visual. Cite both sources in the caption.
- Note: no publisher decorative images. The article's real visual evidence is
  the code's own output (a logit vector with one entry at -inf). None of the
  paper figures should substitute for that.

## Discarded

- https://www.newtuple.com/post/openai-structured-outputs — secondary; reports
  OpenAI's CFG/constrained-decoding mechanism and a "93% → 100% reliability"
  paraphrase. Used only to corroborate the gated OpenAI blog (source 5); not
  citable as a primary. Reason: third-party write-up, no firsthand stake.
- https://www.adambutterworth.com/posts/setting-logits-to-negative-infinity —
  secondary practitioner post. Useful synthesis: a clean logit-mask code
  sketch, a concrete BPE alignment example (`{"name": "Adam"}` → 5 tokens but
  7 grammar transitions), and pointers to jump-forward/coalescence (~1.75x on
  JSON) and SGLang. Discarded as a citation (all its load-bearing facts trace
  to primaries already logged: sources 1, 2, 6, 7, 8), but its BPE example is a
  good model for the tokenizer-alignment section the writer must build itself.
- https://letsdatascience.com/blog/... and
  https://developers.openai.com news-style recaps — secondary; consulted for the
  OpenAI mechanism while the blog was gated. No independent facts.
- https://simonwillison.net/2025/Feb/28/llm-schemas/ (from the voice brief) —
  practitioner secondary; good voice model (the Jsonformer line: compiling the
  schema "into code that interacts with the model's next-token generation at
  runtime, limiting it to only generate tokens that are valid"). Not needed as
  an evidence citation; the mechanism is owned by sources 1–2.
- SGLang (jump-forward decoding, NeurIPS 2024), Guidance (token healing),
  Grammar-Aligned Decoding (NeurIPS 2024) — named by the Adam Butterworth post
  as the origins of coalescence/token-healing. Not opened firsthand this pass;
  flagged for the writer only if the piece decides to cover jump-forward as the
  "overhead constrained decoding can *remove*" angle. If so, they must be read
  before citing.
- OpenAI announcement blog (source 5) — listed here too as the one primary I
  could not read (403 to all fetchers); kept in Sources as GATED rather than
  discarded because its guarantee/limits are corroborated by the readable docs
  (source 4).

## Original work

I hand-built a character-level DFA for the JSON grammar `true | false`, compiled
it against the real 50,257-token GPT-2 vocabulary into a state-to-allowed-token
index, and printed the logit mask's effect on one concrete decoding step: the

by the index while `"true"` rises from 0.36 to 0.85, and shows a single token
crossing four DFA transitions in one step (the tokenizer-alignment point) with
the leading-space variant `" true"` dying immediately.
````
