items.title: feat: memory as a graph, work on a schedule, and a TUI to run it
items.body:
## What this is

Memory becomes a graph, Jod learns to act on its own schedule, and the TUI grows
from a chat window into a control surface for all of it.

**1,163 tests pass, 0 fail** (was 465 on `main` — which, incidentally, did not
compile; see the first commit).

```
                        main            this branch
memory          facts, FTS5      →  + entities/relations graph, trust enforced
time                     —       →  schedules + goals, race-free claim
inbound                  —       →  GitHub webhooks + Telegram
conversation    harness-owned    →  Jod-owned DAG: fork, revert, compact, search
TUI          chat + 2 panels     →  9 workspaces behind a leader key
```

---

## `main` did not compile

PR #42 added `Action::Attach` reading `AgentSummary::attach_command`; PR #43
renamed that field to `watch_command` for the tmux→supervisor move. Each branch
compiled alone. Merged, they did not. Fixed in the first commit.

Worth a CI note: nothing catches a semantic conflict between two green PRs.

---

## The four findings that changed the design

Everything here is graded hypothesis → experiment → measurement. These are the
results that made me build something different from what I'd planned.

### 1. A trust boundary nothing enforced

`facts` has carried an `origin` column since the first migration — `owner`,
`agent`, `untrusted`, `system` — deliberately outside the fact text so ingested
content cannot forge its own trust level.

**Recall never consulted it.** A page Jod merely *fetched* answered exactly as
readily as something Reljod said. Measured against a hand-labelled corpus: the
poisoned fact came back on **10% of queries**.

The column, the doc comment and the migration comment all described a control
that did not exist. Found by measuring shipped behaviour, not by re-reading the
design.

Verified live after the fix:

```
$ jod remember reljod uses jod
remembered #1
# an untrusted fact injected directly into the store:
$ jod recall claims
nothing remembered about that
```

**This claim was wrong when first written, and is now true.** It said untrusted
material was excluded from graph *seeding* too. It was not: `recall_expanded` had
the filter and nothing in production called it, while `jod related` and `jod path`
walk the edges directly — so an ingested page's assertion sat one hop from a real
entity and came back. Fixed by never building the edge: an untrusted fact is
stored and searchable with an explicit flag, and is not linked into the graph at
all, on insert or on rebuild. Filtering at read means every read has to remember;
not building the edge means none of them do.

### 2. `JOIN` is a 64× pessimisation in a recursive CTE

The graph research benchmarked the design in Python. Run through the real
`Store`, the published query text made SQLite invert the join order: `relations`
became the outer loop matched on `scope` alone — selecting every row — with the
frontier scanned inside it. It also used the in-edge index for *both*
directions, so the out-edge index was never touched.

| 2-hop, 10k edges | p50 |
|---|---|
| `JOIN` (as designed) | **903 ms** |
| `CROSS JOIN` | **14 ms** |

Same schema, same indexes. It fails *silently* — correct, just quadratic — so
tests pass and it degrades as memory grows.

**I also corrected the headline number.** The research advertises 0.37 ms for
3 hops at 1M edges; that is the *directed* traversal. "What is related to this"
is undirected, needs two recursive terms, and measures **92 ms p50 at 100k**.
Both correct, only one is ours. The conclusion held, but on the real figure.
→ `research/sqlite-graph-2026/MEASURED.md`, re-runnable via
`cargo run --release --example graph_bench`.

### 3. A lease alone loses one claim in five

Sixteen processes racing for due schedules: a read-then-write claim handed the
**same schedule to two winners 41.26% of the time**; the guarded single
statement gave **0 duplicates in 5,408 claims**.

The non-obvious part is crash recovery. A lease *looks* sufficient — it expires,
someone takes over. But the next claimant **overwrites** the lease, and the
original claim then exists in no record at all: **52 of 255 claims, one in
five**. The reaper arrives to find nothing to reap. Making the claim record the
abandonment *before* taking it: **0 of 270**.

### 4. Jitter sounded prudent and measured worse

Across ten graded scheduler iterations, jitter is the only addition that made
things worse: a 300 s spread against a 150 s grace window **lost 34 of 72 fires**
outright. Iteration 8 ranks *below* iterations 6 and 7 despite being later and
larger — which is the entire argument for scoring iterations rather than taking
the newest.

Ships defaulting to zero, and refused at the boundary when wider than grace.

---

## What is built

**Memory graph** — `entities`/`relations` as a derived index over `facts`, in the
same `jod.db`. On the "SQLite graph extension" ask, the answer is a justified
**no**: none is simultaneously maintained in 2026, permissively licensed *and*
statically linkable into one binary. Bitemporal filtering measured *free* (87 ms
filtered vs 92 ms unfiltered — pruning an edge costs less than expanding it).
`forget` cascades to edges, so "Jod forgot that" still means "Jod says it forgot
that".

**Schedules and goals** — croner (the only crate of four correct on *both* DST
transitions; `cron` and `cronexpr` fire a daily job twice across fall-back).
IANA zone names, never offsets. Misfire, overlap, backoff and a breaker, each
sized by simulation. Goals carry **stall detection** — a loop completing
iterations while nothing changes is the characteristic autonomous failure, and
from outside it looks identical to working hard.

**Conversations** — a DAG with a moving head, the shape git/ChatGPT/LangGraph
converged on and the harnesses did not. Fork, non-destructive revert, compaction
as a first-class node, FTS5 search with bookends.

**Webhooks** — HMAC over raw bytes before parsing, constant-time compare,
delivery-id dedupe, fail-closed when unconfigured, payload treated as hostile.

**Telegram** — default-deny allowlist, UTF-16-correct chunking at 4096.

**TUI** — nine workspaces behind `Ctrl-K`. Selection is by **id, not row index**:
the fleet re-sorts every four ticks, so an index would move the cursor onto a
different agent at the moment one finishes — exactly when you're about to press
`s` or `⏎`.

---

## Reversing a stated design

`docs/jod-system.md` asserted *"Jod needs no memory of the transcript: the
harness owns it."* Probing the three binaries:

| | Claude Code | OpenCode | AGY |
|---|---|---|---|
| fork | `--fork-session` | `--fork` | **none** |
| export | — | `opencode export` | none |
| import | `--input-format stream-json` | `opencode import` | none |

Two can fork themselves, so Jod delegates that. **None can hand a thread to
another**, and AGY can do neither — so cross-harness handoff has no owner unless
Jod is one. The doc now says it was wrong rather than quietly dropping the
sentence. → `docs/decisions.md`

---

## Known gaps, stated plainly

- **Telegram is untested against a live token** — the pure logic (chunking,
  escaping, session keying, allowlist, backoff) is covered; the network path is
  not, and I would not fake a credential to claim otherwise.
- **`reqwest`+rustls pulls `aws-lc-sys`**, a heavyweight C dependency. It builds
  here, but it is at odds with "one static binary on a plain VPS" and deserves a
  second look at the TLS backend.
- **Goal iterations do not yet write their episodic record.** The scope and the
  schema are there and the design is in `docs/decisions.md`; the write is not.
- Hermes parity: **matched** on memory, chat and scheduling, and its two best
  ideas — monitor-hash suppression and the delivery ledger — are now built.
  Not built: consent-first job suggestions, blueprints, the curator.

## Proven by running it, not only by tests

```
$ jod schedule add tick-demo "echo hello" --cron "*/5 * * * *"
tick-demo armed — next Aug 10 20:55 (in 2s)

$ jod daemon --once
claimed 1 · started 0 · held 0 · failed 1

$ jod schedule log tick-demo
✗ spawn_failed   the `jod-run` supervisor was not found
```

That failure earns its place: the run did not happen and the record says so with
the reason, rather than leaving silence. With the supervisor on PATH:

```
claimed 1 · started 1 · held 0 · failed 0
✓ ran
"status": "completed", "last_message": "hello"
```

A real Claude Code harness, started by the scheduler, on a schedule.

Also verified against the release binary: a schedule armed in `Asia/Manila`
computes 02:00 local as 18:00 UTC; a paused schedule refuses `run` rather than
firing silently; `jod related reljod -n 3` walks `jod → jod-cloud → hetzner`
from three facts written one at a time; and an untrusted fact injected straight
into the store does not surface in `jod recall`.


## Evidence

- `cargo test --workspace` → **1,163 passed, 0 failed**
- `cargo run --release --example graph_bench` → the graph numbers
- `research/*/out/` → raw measurements, re-runnable
- Ten graded iterations per track with ranking tables in `research/*/REPORT.md`

Two subagents hit a harness hook forbidding them to write report files. Both
filed `BLOCKED.md` and returned findings as text rather than routing around the
check with a shell heredoc — the correct reading of the charter. Those reports
were written by the lead session from their committed raw output.


---

# Added after the description above was written

## The main chat

One pinned conversation that never ends, and the place instructions go.

```sh
jod main "every weekday at 8am, sweep the open PRs and tell me what needs me"
jod main "keep working until the README explains what jod main does, then stop"
jod main "count the Rust files in the repo and tell me"
jod main                                  # read it back
```

It does not do the work. It is a harness run holding Jod's own tools over MCP,
so it delegates by *calling* rather than by describing, and returns in the same
second it was typed.

Four instructions, four routes, none of them hinted at:

| instruction | tool it called | result |
|---|---|---|
| "Every weekday at 8am Asia/Manila…" | `schedule_create` | `weekday-pr-sweep`, armed |
| "keep working until… then stop" | `goal_create` | `readme-explains-jod-main`, running |
| "Count how many Rust source files…" | `delegate` | new run `31ca3ac4` |
| "Follow up on that Rust file count…" | `continue_agent` | `{"continued":"31ca3ac4…","run_id":"b21e64f2…"}` |

The last row is the one worth having. `continue_agent` resumed the existing
agent's session, so the follow-up prompt already contained the count — it did not
recount. Full transcript in [`tests/e2e/main-chat/REPORT.md`](tests/e2e/main-chat/REPORT.md).

### It took four runs to get one tool call through

Every failure was a component that was complete, tested, and connected to
nothing. All four are in `docs/decisions.md`; the pair worth repeating:

**`PermissionPolicy::Ask` is plan mode, and plan mode refuses the MCP write
tools too.** The orchestrator called `schedule_list`, `list_agents` and `recall`,
reached for `ExitPlanMode`, and wrote a plan file instead of arming the schedule.
That looked like a model that would not commit; it was a mode that would not let
it. The confinement axis (what a run may do to the *machine*) and the grant axis
(what it may do to *Jod*) are separate, and the code now says so.

**Which exposed the next one immediately:** the `mcp__jod` entry in
`--allowedTools` had been written inside the `Ask` arm, so moving off plan mode
silently revoked every Jod tool — four consecutive *"requested permissions to use
`mcp__jod__schedule_create`, but you haven't granted it yet"*.

The test that missed it is the interesting part. It asserted the grant appears —
under `Ask`, the only mode it ever passed. **A test that fixes one value of the
variable your bug lives in passes forever.** It now loops over every permission
mode.

Also added: `SpawnRequest::system`, so standing framing is a system prompt rather
than the conversation's opening user turn. Claude Code takes
`--append-system-prompt`; harnesses without one have it folded into the prompt by
the runner.

## Webhooks were unreachable

The receiver, the HMAC check, the condition matcher, the delivery ledger and the
TUI's rule list with its enable/disable/delete keys were all built and tested.
`add_webhook_rule` had **no production caller** — only test functions. The
`webhook_rules` table was empty on every real machine, every delivery matched
nothing, and the feature could not be used while every test was green.

`jod webhook add|ls|enable|disable|rm|deliveries` is the missing verb. Proven
against a live `jod-api` with real HMAC-signed bodies —
[`tests/e2e/webhook/REPORT.md`](tests/e2e/webhook/REPORT.md):

| case | HTTP | ledger |
|---|---|---|
| matches the rule | 202 | `accepted`, agent started |
| wrong label / action / repo | 200 | `no_match` |
| forged signature | **401** | `rejected` |

A rejected delivery is still recorded. "GitHub says it delivered, Jod has no
record" is the alternative.

What the stranger's agent actually got, from run `b5c9d705`'s spawn plan: values
as quoted JSON literals, `--permission-mode plan`, and **no `--mcp-config`** — so
nothing a stranger writes can reach `schedule_create`.

## One byte made a module invisible to every audit

`core/src/webhook.rs` held a literal NUL inside a doc comment — in the line
explaining how control bytes are escaped. Valid UTF-8, so rustc accepted it and
its 39 tests passed. But `grep` classifies a file containing NUL as binary and
skips it silently: no warning, no partial result, no output, exit 0.

So for that module, every `grep -rn` in this branch returned nothing — including
the ones that concluded a function had no callers. **`wiring.py`, the audit that
produced this branch's sharpest finding ("44 of 278 core pub fns have no
production caller"), never saw 1,234 lines of it.** `match_rules` appearing to be
called from `api/` and defined nowhere is what finally exposed it.

The lesson is not about NUL bytes. A silent zero and a true zero are
indistinguishable, and every "nothing calls this" was resting on that ambiguity.

## Smaller, but it was lying to the user

`jod ls` shows an eight-character id and `jod main` prints ``jod watch 1f0fc870``
as a hint — while `jod watch` and `jod kill` both demanded the full uuid. The
hint the tool printed did not work. Both now resolve a prefix through one
`resolve_run`, refusing an ambiguous prefix rather than guessing.

Transcript rendering too: a `schedule_create` turn showed as
`{"cron":"0 8 * * 1-5","cwd":"/home/reljod","misfire":…` and its result as an
escaped content array. Now `schedule_create weekday-pr-sweep`. Tool calls read
from `tool_input` because `text` is a *summary*, cut mid-string with a
`… (+926 chars)` marker glued on, so it is not JSON and no parsing will make it
one.

## The TUI reaches it too

`/main <instruction>` (or `/jod`) in the chat workspace hands the line to the
orchestrator and watches the run, so the routing decision and its reason land on
screen. It calls `crate::hand_to_orchestrator` — **the same function `jod main`
calls**, not a TUI-shaped copy. Which conversation, which tools and which
permission mode are decisions with four bugs already behind them; a second copy
would be a second place for the fifth to hide.

## Still not done

- **Telegram is untested against a live token.** Unchanged, and it needs a
  credential I will not fake.
- **`orchestrate` has never been granted to anything but the main chat.**
- **`jod monitor` does not exist**, so schedule monitors cannot be created —
  the same gap `jod webhook` just closed, one table over.
- **Goal iterations still do not write their episodic record.**


---

# Second pass: the modes, the screen, and the ledger

32 further commits. **15 suites, 1410 tests, 0 failures.** Core functions with no
production caller: **37 → 15**, while 23 new ones were added.

## The reason nothing Jod started was ever allowed to act

`PermissionPolicy::Ask` mapped to Claude Code's `--permission-mode plan` **and**
was `#[default]`. So the default for every spawn — the chat box, a schedule at
2am, a goal iteration, a webhook run — was planning mode. Jod could describe work
in any amount of detail and could not do any of it, which reads as a model being
unhelpful rather than as a flag.

Four levels now, split so that "think, do not act" and "act, but check with me"
are different things:

| | claude | opencode | agy |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Plan` | `--permission-mode plan` | — | `--mode plan` |
| `Ask` | `--permission-mode manual` | — | — (its default is ask) |
| `AcceptEdits` | `--permission-mode acceptEdits` | — | `--mode accept-edits` |
| `Bypass` ("auto") | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` | `--auto` | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` |

Flag names read off `claude --help`, `agy --help` and `opencode run --help`, not
assumed — a prior attempt at this seam had designed around
`--permission-prompt-tool`, which this build does not have. A test pins every
mode Jod emits against the six the binary accepts. OpenCode genuinely cannot
express three of the four and says so rather than emitting a `--mode plan` it
would ignore.

**Then it turned out `jod run` never saw the fix.** `cli/src/main.rs` had a
second `PermissionArg` enum duplicating the level list — the exact drift its
neighbour `parse_access_arg` carries a comment warning about. It never learned
the fourth mode and its default stayed `ask`:

```
$ jod run -H claude "Create a file called proof.txt containing exactly ACTED"
✗ Write
The write needs your permission — the request is waiting for approval.
$ ls /tmp/jod-modecheck/          # empty
```

One parser in core now. After:

```
$ jod run -H claude --cwd /tmp/jod-modecheck "Create proof.txt containing ACTED"
⚙ Write
Created `/tmp/jod-modecheck/proof.txt` containing `ACTED`.
✓ done · $0.0428 · 131 out
$ cat /tmp/jod-modecheck/proof.txt
ACTED
```

And the converse still holds — `-p plan` refuses and writes a plan instead, with
the directory left empty. Found by running the binary; no unit test would have.

## Memory that is read back

`recall::augment` injects remembered facts as a **system-prompt preamble** at
`spawn_agent_in` — the one call every spawn funnels through, so a schedule
recalls as well as a chat. `Origin::Untrusted` facts are never injected;
superseded facts are not; the preamble is bounded by a named constant.

```
$ jod remember "reljod" "prefers" "linear for tasks, never a shadow copy" --origin owner
remembered #2
$ jod run -H claude "Where should reljod's tasks live? One sentence."
In Linear — as real issues on the team's board, not a shadow copy elsewhere.
```

## The delivery ledger: 11 unwired functions to zero

`core/src/ledger.rs` was 927 lines, fully tested, and connected to nothing — its
own header said so: *"Today nothing anywhere records the difference"* between a
notification delivered and one that was not.

Now wired at both ends, plus `jod ledger ls|show|failed`:

```
◐ attempting Deploy finished. Rollback window closes in 30 minutes.
  telegram→7:99 · Aug 11 17:27 (9m59s ago) · 1 attempt · telegram:7:42
  in flight — if the process holding it died, this is resent labelled a possible duplicate
● delivered  The nightly digest is ready: 3 PRs merged, 1 blocked on review.
  telegram→7 · Aug 11 15:09 (2h40m ago) · 1 attempt · telegram:7:41
  resent after a crash Aug 11 15:49 — the recipient may hold two copies
✗ failed     Weekly summary attached.
  telegram→7 · Aug 10 13:50 (27h46m ago) · 3 attempts · telegram:7:44
  Unauthorized: bot was removed from the chat
```

Two briefs I wrote were wrong and were refused before being built:

- **Sweeping from `Daemon::persistent`.** `jod daemon` holds no transport, and
  `sweep_recoverable` claims as it reads. A daemon sweep would take every
  orphaned row, send none, then be *alive* — so every later sweep correctly
  skips them. It converts recoverable rows into permanently stranded ones.
- **Leaving `sweep_recoverable` without a channel filter.** Measured, not
  reasoned: a `cli` row in front of a telegram bridge is `failed` after **three
  restarts**, because the redelivery path spends an attempt before discovering it
  cannot address the row. Not stranded — destroyed, by a process that never
  attempted delivery and never could have.

Migration `0012` verified against a copy of the real `~/.jod/jod.db` (471 KB,
populated), not a fixture: applied cleanly, existing facts intact.

## The screen

- **Alt keymap.** Ctrl chords collided with tmux, whose own prefix is `Ctrl-B` —
  which was Jod's delegate key, so that binding never arrived at all. Alt for
  Jod's verbs; `Ctrl-A/E/U/W/C/D` stay where every terminal already puts them.
  A test now presses what the screen prints, so the display table and the
  dispatch cannot drift.
- **The keybar was dropping the way out.** `two_ends` reserved room for the
  verbs and sacrificed the right-hand half — at 80 columns Chat, Fleet and Memory
  all stopped saying `Esc back · ? keys`. **Every render test in the suite was
  150 wide**, which is why it survived in plain sight. The exit is now reserved
  first; verbs are budgeted and announce truncation with `? more`; `?` carries
  the rest.
- Two more of the same shape: `keys::footer` clipped mid-word (`… r resume · d d`)
  in the ~92–140 band, and the `?` overlay silently dropped 18 rows at 80×30.
- **Splash, panel, context box.** Centred `Jod AI` on a new session; Shift-Tab
  opens a right-hand panel; a lower-right box graphs context used and says when
  to compact, labelled as an estimate because Jod cannot know the real window.
- **Modes are visible and changeable.** Tab cycles, `/mode` names one, colour
  plus glyph plus word so `NO_COLOR` loses decoration and never information.
  The `--permission` flag is now a **ceiling** the TUI may not exceed.

## Other things closed

- **Telegram is one durable conversation** per chat, with `/new`, `/clear`,
  `/help`. The mapping outlived the process only after this — it was a `HashMap`,
  so a restart silently started every chat over.
- **The bot token was being written to the log in clear text**, via a reqwest
  error containing the URL. Redacted where the error is built, not where it is
  printed, because there is no single place it is printed.
- **A turn you are watching can arm a schedule.** The chat box passed
  `tools: None`, so Jod could acknowledge "schedule this" and had no verb to do
  it. `WATCHED` gets `Orchestrate`; `DELEGATED` gets `ToolAccess::unattended()`.
- **`/model` and `/mode` persist on the conversation**, so a resume comes back as
  you left it. Switching harness compacts and carries the summary across.
- **Branch, fork, revert and go-to are reachable** from the fleet, so an
  abandoned branch is findable by name rather than by remembering an integer.
- **`jod monitor`** exists, closing one of this PR's own "still not done" items.

## Still not done

- **The Telegram round trip is unproven.** The bridge runs and polls cleanly as
  `@jod_ai_bot`; nobody has messaged it. Needs a person, not a credential.
- **Goal iterations still do not write their episodic record.**
- **The ledger has no TUI surface** — `jod ledger` is the only way in, so the
  fleet cannot say "this run's reply never arrived", which is the question asked
  from the screen you are most likely to be standing on.
- 15 core functions still have no production caller.

## What this branch kept getting wrong

Every failure above is one shape: **something complete, tested, and connected to
nothing.** `tools` reached no command line; monitors had no way to be created;
Telegram had no entry point; the ledger had eleven unwired functions; preferences
were written and never read back. Unit tests were green throughout each one.

`tests/e2e/jod/wiring.py` is the only thing that reliably finds them, and it
moved 37 → 15 here. The second recurring shape, added to `docs/teamwork.md` after
four instances in one session: **verifying a claim about behaviour means finding
the call site — a function's body is where you go second.** Three were checks
aimed at the wrong place. The fourth was a check that never happened, because the
reviewer recognised his own reasoning arriving in someone else's words and graded
it as corroboration.

items.title: v2.1.2: SIMD/SHA3 fixes, Ed25519 AVX2 dispatch & optimization, benchmarks
items.body: ## Summary Release v2.1.2 addresses critical correctness bugs in SIMD implementations (SVE2 NTT, NEON SHA3), fixes file descriptor leaks, improves CI/CD workflows, adds proper licensing for vendored ed25519-donna library, **wires Ed25519 into the AVX2 dispatch system with scalar multiplication optimizations**, and **runs a full benchmark suite with updated results and regenerated visuals**. ### Updates since last revision - **README.md audit** (11eb2ab): Full audit of README benchmark numbers against committed source-of-truth files (`benchmark-results.json`, `benchmarks/phase0_baseline_results.json`). Key corrections: - All benchmark tables now show **verified Python API (ctypes) throughput** from `benchmark-results.json` with explicit source attribution - ML-DSA-65: corrected to 595/567/697 ops/sec (keygen/sign/verify) — previous README had unverifiable C/Py split numbers - Core primitives: corrected to match regression suite (e.g. SHA3-256 1KB: 18,205 ops/sec, Ed25519 Sign: 5,069 ops/sec) - Package Create/Verify: corrected to 184/561 ops/sec - ML-KEM-1024, Scalability, Ethical overhead tables: replaced unverified numbers with "measure locally" instructions - Blockchain section: ML-DSA-65 latency corrected from ~0.97ms/~0.20ms to ~1.76ms/~1.43ms - Install instructions: `pip install -r requirements.txt` → `pip install -e ".[dev]"` - Test count: 1,264 → 1,855+ - "What We Did Right" → "Design Principles" (less self-assessment tone) - Version ref `v2.1` → `v2.1.2` - **Wiki version consistency fix** (e8d423a): Updated 3 wiki files (`Home.md`, `Security-Model.md`, `_Footer.md`) from `2.1.0` → `2.1.2` to match the actual release version across all other locations. Also fixed the CHANGELOG entry (line 46) that incorrectly described this as "consistent `2.1.0` format". Addressed Devin Review comments [#3037874157, #3037874180, #3037874205] individually. ### Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [x] Security fix (addresses a security vulnerability) - [x] Performance optimization (Ed25519 stack allocation, binary cmov table lookup) - [x] Code refactoring (improves code quality without changing functionality) - [x] Documentation update (benchmark numbers, charts, README audit, wiki version refs) ### Related Issues Fixes #318 (file descriptor leak in legacy_compat.py) Fixes #333 (unused static function CodeQL alert) ## Motivation and Context ### Why is this change required? This release fixes critical data corruption bugs in SIMD implementations, resolves resource leaks, improves CI/CD security posture, establishes proper licensing attribution, **optimizes Ed25519 performance**, and **updates all benchmark documentation with verified measured values aligned to committed data files**. ### What problem does it solve? 1. **SVE2 NTT correctness:** Missing `lo_buf` store in butterfly operation caused silent data corruption on AArch64 SVE2 platforms 2. **NEON SHA3 Chi step:** Unused NEON vectors masked incorrect scalar implementation 3. **File descriptor leak:** `os.open()` file descriptors not guaranteed to close on exception 4. **CI/CD security:** Direct commits to protected branches replaced with PR-based workflow 5. **Licensing compliance:** ed25519-donna attribution and license file added 6. **Ed25519 performance:** Heap allocation per sign/verify call and O(n) table lookup in scalar multiplication 7. **Stale benchmark data:** README contained numbers with no backing data file — now all numbers trace to `benchmark-results.json` or `phase0_baseline_results.json` ## Cryptographic Impact ### Security Impact Assessment - [x] Modifies existing cryptographic operation (requires security analysis) - [x] Performance optimization only (no security changes) ### Standards Compliance - [x] NIST FIPS 202 (SHA-3) - [x] NIST FIPS 204 (Dilithium / ML-DSA-65) - [x] NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM-1024) - [x] RFC 8032 (Ed25519) ### Security Analysis **Classical Security:** The SVE2 NTT bug could produce incorrect polynomial multiplications in Dilithium signatures. The fix restores correct NTT computation. NEON SHA3 Chi step fix ensures correct Keccak-f[1600] permutation on ARM NEON platforms. Ed25519 optimizations maintain constant-time properties — binary cmov table lookup touches all 16 entries via 4 binary decomposition layers, and stack allocation has no secret-dependent branching. **Quantum Security:** No impact to quantum security posture. Fixes maintain post-quantum algorithm correctness. ## Implementation Details ### Changes Made (Task 1 — Review Fixes) 1. **SVE2 NTT correctness** (`src/c/sve2/ama_dilithium_sve2.c`): Added missing `lo_buf` store in butterfly 2. **NEON SHA3 Chi step** (`src/c/neon/ama_sha3_neon.c`): Removed dead NEON loads, updated comment to say chi uses scalar ops 3. **SHA2 header** (`src/c/internal/ama_sha2.h`): Added `#include ` 4. **AVX2 Dilithium** (`src/c/avx2/ama_dilithium_avx2.c`): Added `AMA_UNUSED` annotation 5. **File descriptor leak** (`ama_cryptography/legacy_compat.py`): Restructured to try/with pattern 6. **Duplicate super().run()** (`setup.py`): Ensured exactly one `super().run()` call 7. **Sentinel filtering** (`setup.py`): Removed unnecessary `_ama_cmake_sentinel` filter 8. **CI build isolation** (`.github/workflows/ci-build-test.yml`): Dropped `--no-build-isolation` 9. **CHANGELOG ARM64/QEMU claim**: Removed false claim 10. **Version bump to 2.1.2**: All 5 locations updated + wiki (3 files) fixed in follow-up commit ### Changes Made (Task 2 — Ed25519 AVX2 Dispatch & Optimization) 1. **Dispatch wiring** (`include/ama_dispatch.h`, `src/c/dispatch/ama_dispatch.c`): - Added Ed25519 function pointer typedefs (keypair, sign, verify) and fields to `ama_dispatch_table_t` - Wire AVX2 path in `dispatch_init_internal()` when AVX2 is detected 2. **AVX2 wrapper functions** (`src/c/avx2/ama_ed25519_avx2.c`): - Added `ama_ed25519_keypair_avx2`, `ama_ed25519_sign_avx2`, `ama_ed25519_verify_avx2` - Currently delegate to optimized generic implementation; AVX2 field ops available for future vectorized scalar mult 3. **Stack allocation in sign/verify** (`src/c/ama_ed25519.c`): - `ED25519_STACK_THRESHOLD = 4096` — messages ≤4KB use stack buffer, larger messages heap-allocate - Eliminates malloc/free per call for >99% of real-world messages 4. **Binary cmov table lookup** (`src/c/ama_ed25519.c`): - Replaced 16-iteration linear scan with 4-layer binary decomposition conditional move - Reduces XOR operations from 320 to 80 per scalar mult nibble - All code remains constant-time (no secret-dependent branches) ### Changes Made (Task 3 — Benchmarks, Visuals, Compliance) 1. **Benchmark results** (measured, not fabricated): - Ed25519 Sign: **13,100 ops/sec** (C) / **8,923 ops/sec** (Python API) - Ed25519 Verify: **6,635 ops/sec** (C) / **4,748 ops/sec** (Py) - ML-KEM-1024 Encaps: **11,905 ops/sec** (C) - ML-DSA-65 Verify: **6,855 ops/sec** (C) / **4,137 ops/sec** (Py) 2. **Regenerated 5 SVG charts** in `benchmarks/charts/` with updated data 3. **Fixed `generate_charts.py` bug**: KeyError on `'SHA3-256 (short)'` (dict key was `'SHA3-256 (1KB)'`) 4. **Updated README.md** benchmark section with both Python API and raw C throughput 5. **Compliance verified**: FIPS POST 34/34, KAT 49/49 (815 NIST vectors), integrity digest OK, bandit 0 issues ### Changes Made (README Audit) Aligned all README benchmark numbers to committed data files. The C raw numbers from Task 3 (e.g. Ed25519 Sign 13,100 ops/sec) were measured live but **not saved to a committed JSON file**, so the README now shows only the CI regression suite numbers from `benchmark-results.json`. See "Important note on benchmark numbers" below. ## Testing - **Python tests:** 1848 passed, 7 skipped - **C tests:** 8/8 passed via ctest - **KAT vectors:** 49/49 passed (815 NIST vectors across 6 standards) - **FIPS 140-3 POST:** 34/34 passed - **Module integrity:** verified - **Security scans:** bandit 0 issues - **CI:** 77/77 checks passing (includes CodeQL, ASan+UBSan, fuzz, dudect, all platform matrices) ## Review & Testing Checklist - [ ] **Benchmark number discrepancy — README vs Task 3 live measurements:** The README now shows `benchmark-results.json` numbers (CI shared runner, Python API via ctypes — e.g. Ed25519 Sign: 5,069 ops/sec). Task 3 measured higher numbers locally (e.g. 13,100 C / 8,923 Py). The C raw numbers were never committed to a data file. **Decide whether to:** (a) accept README showing only regression-suite numbers, (b) re-run benchmarks and commit a `c_benchmark_results.json` to back the higher C numbers, or (c) add both sets with clear labels. - [ ] **Verify constant-time properties of binary cmov table lookup** (`src/c/ama_ed25519.c:525-565`): The 4-layer binary decomposition and nibble==0 identity override must not introduce timing leaks. Consider running `dudect` or equivalent timing analysis against this path. - [ ] **Review stack allocation threshold** (`ED25519_STACK_THRESHOLD = 4096`): Confirm 4KB+ stack frames in `ama_ed25519_sign` and `ama_ed25519_verify` are acceptable for all target platforms (embedded, threaded, recursive callers). - [ ] **Confirm AVX2 dispatch wiring is safe when NULL**: The dispatch table entries are NULL on non-AVX2 platforms — verify all callers NULL-check before calling (grep for `dispatch_table.ed25519_`). - [ ] **Spot-check version consistency**: Verify `2.1.2` appears in all 8 locations (pyproject.toml, setup.py, `__init__.py`, README.md, legacy_compat.py, wiki/Home.md, wiki/Security-Model.md, wiki/_Footer.md). **Recommended test plan:** 1. Build with `cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DAMA_BUILD_TESTS=ON && cmake --build build -j$(nproc)` 2. Run `cd build && ctest --output-on-failure` (expect 8/8) 3. Run `pip install -e . && python -m pytest tests/ -q` (expect 1848+ passed) 4. Run `python benchmark_suite.py` and compare Ed25519 ops/sec against baseline (~5K → improvement expected) 5. Run `python -c "from ama_cryptography.integrity import verify_module_integrity; assert verify_module_integrity()"` 6. Render README.md on GitHub and verify benchmark tables, collapsible sections, and links render correctly ### Notes - **Important note on benchmark numbers:** The README previously contained benchmark numbers from two sources: (1) `build/bin/benchmark_c_raw` (raw C, higher numbers) and (2) `python benchmark_suite.py` (Python API, lower numbers). Only the Python API numbers are tracked in `benchmark-results.json`. The README audit aligned all numbers to this committed file. To restore C-vs-Python comparisons, run `build/bin/benchmark_c_raw` and commit the output to a JSON file. - The AVX2 Ed25519 wrapper functions currently delegate to the optimized generic C implementation. The existing AVX2 fe51 field arithmetic (`ama_fe51_mul_avx2`, `ama_fe51_sq_avx2`) is available for a future fully-vectorized scalar multiplication path. - Semgrep reported 1043 findings — these are from pre-existing codebase rules, not newly introduced. - The `generate_charts.py` baseline data was updated to match actual measurements. These are environment-specific; running on different hardware will produce different numbers. Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/a3ac12dbf9bc44e1a3c12833eb406c58 Requested by: @Steel-SecAdv-LLC ---

items.title: feat(wfgg): workflow_graphgen A-vs-A+B benchmark + real n=10 measurement
items.body:
## What

Builds the `workflow_graphgen` A-vs-A+B benchmark and runs a **real, variance-aware n=10 measurement** of it with Sonnet-4.6.

The single independent variable is **who executes the dynamic middle graph**:
- **Mode A** — the Python runner walks the middle graph (engine-dispatched).
- **Mode A+B** — the harness loops `ir.middle_chain()` and calls `_codergen(Node(...))` per node directly.

Everything else is held fixed: shared graph-IR, identical `baseline_ref` handoff, identical coder backend/model, and a coder prompt that is **byte-identical across modes** (templates interpolate only `${goal}` — guarded by a unit test).

## Headline result — no separation on any axis at n=10

40 real Sonnet runs (10 trials × hello/roman × A/A+B), middle-only, conformance graded against the **public** acceptance criteria.

| Feature | Axis | A (mean ± sd) | A+B (mean ± sd) | Verdict |
|--------|------|---------------|-----------------|---------|
| hello | conformance | 1.00 ± 0.00 | 1.00 ± 0.00 | **tie** (50/50) |
| hello | tokens_total | 281 910 ± 27 175 | 281 398 ± 38 755 | no separation |
| hello | wall_ms | 41 373 ± 3 873 | 43 550 ± 6 030 | A+B +5.3%, overlaps |
| roman | conformance | 1.00 ± 0.00 | 1.00 ± 0.00 | **tie** (90/90) |
| roman | tokens_total | 304 748 ± 39 946 | 313 719 ± 38 618 | no separation |
| roman | wall_ms | 48 700 ± 3 637 | 53 190 ± 4 868 | A+B +9.2%, overlaps |

**Practical read:** for first-pass coding tasks the dispatch path is a wash on correctness and cost; Mode A has a marginal latency edge (no offsetting benefit). No winner is credited.

## Why this is a real measurement, not an n=1 point estimate

- The earlier n=1 smoke showed "A cheaper on hello / A+B cheaper on roman" — that was **pure model variance** (sd ≈ 27k–40k tokens). At n=10 the ranges overlap and the signal vanishes.
- New `MIN_N_FOR_WINNER=5` + range-non-overlap guard **correctly refused to crown that false winner**.
- Token axis is uncounfounded (byte-identical prompt, parity test).

## Instrument added
- `conformance_local.py` — self-contained evaluator grading hello/roman against their **public** acceptance criteria (no sealed repo, no agent-isolation break).
- `scoring.py` — `MIN_N_FOR_WINNER=5` guard, per-mode variance stats, `wall_ms` axis.
- `--conformance local` + `--spine`/`--no-spine` (core measurement runs middle-only to isolate the variable).
- `RESULTS.md` + raw evidence under `results/`.
- 18 new instrument tests; **full suite 153 green**.

## Scope / honesty caveats
- `graph_quality` can **never** separate A from A+B — both consume the same IR (mode-invariant by construction).
- hello/roman are easy, first-pass tasks. A null result does **not** generalize to fix-loop tasks where A+B's per-node control could diverge — that is the next experiment.

## Design doc / bead
N/A — this is a benchmark in the `dark-factory` runner repo (layer-1), not `mvp_site/**` production code; the `design-doc-gate` / bead policy targets `worldarchitect.ai`.

## Evidence
UI: `N/A - no UI behavior changed`. Raw artifacts committed at `benchmarks/workflow_graphgen/results/n10_records.jsonl` + `n10_aggregate.json`; reproduce command in `RESULTS.md`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes the production Claude codergen invocation (JSON output, model_name) and gate verdict parsing; benchmarks are additive but the handler path is shared by real pipeline runs.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds the **workflow_graphgen** benchmark stack (graph-IR, `prompts/catalog.json`, harness for Mode A vs A+B, local conformance, `scoring.aggregate` with `MIN_N_FOR_WINNER=5`) plus committed **n=10 Sonnet** evidence showing no credited winner on conformance/tokens/wall time for hello/roman.
> 
> Adds **dynamic_fanout** as a deterministic sibling benchmark (shared aggregator, G3 runtime fan-out vs static `.dot`, parametric `sweep.py`) and **`benchmarks/FINDINGS.md`** with the decision rule: static graphs by default; fan-out only when **K** is runtime-known.
> 
> **Runner:** Claude `codergen` now uses `--output-format json`, optional node **`model_name`** → `--model`, and **`_claude_json_result`** for token/cost metadata; gate **verdict** regex is tightened so prose like “not a fail” is not mis-parsed.
>

## Intent Land Alessandro Boni's five accepted commits on main (PRs 20, 21, 23, 18, 25) with authorship intact ## What Changed - `src/reasonsmith/demo.py` gains four end-to-end demonstration sections — EU AI Act Art. 13 deployer information (row 1), EU AI Act Art. 12 automatic record-keeping (row 2), FDA GMLP SaMD lifecycle transparency (row 5), and NIST AI RMF 1.0 continuous risk monitoring (row 6) — so `python -m reasonsmith.demo` now covers all six Table 7 rows. Each builds its evidence record from the reason-deletion certificate rather than beside it: Art. 13's `fidelity_coverage_metrics` is computed from the certificate, and the Art. 12 log entry records the active constraint set alongside the chosen branch and marks violation status as not assessed rather than implying clean. `stability_demo` was refactored onto the shared `drift_windows` helper the new NIST section uses, keeping its output byte-identical. - Docs re-measured against the new transcript: `docs/example-output.md` carries the regenerated 905-line demo stdout (sections 6–9 added, `md5sum 954ba56adb96646647b63aae147b0c2b`), with the RESULTS.md line-count/md5 figures updated as a new dated measurement while the historical Repin and PyPI notes keep the 561-line figures they actually recorded. README's architecture table now lists all six demos and documents that `stratified()` output is JSON-native with unmeasured metrics serialising as `null`, never `0`; CONTRIBUTING moves the remaining open work to the `probed` engine and wider temporal monitor rule sets. - `tests/test_reasonsmith.py` adds 11 tests over the new sections — evidence-field shape, log-entry content, determinism, and the stability alert — and `tests/test_docs_example_output.py` continues to re-run every command block in the docs and compare stdout byte for byte. Addresses #6: the four Table 7 duties it lists are now demonstrated end-to-end in `src/reasonsmith/demo.py`. Not closing the issue here. All five upstream commits from @SandroHub013 (PRs 20, 21, 23, 18, 25) land with their original authorship intact; the follow-up commits are adaptation to the current tree, review fixes, and doc sync. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: The round-1 provenance defects are fully corrected with historical figures restored and new figures recorded in a separately dated note, the code changes are behavior-preserving deduplication and import hoisting, and the intent's authorship requirement is satisfied across all six contributor commits with no AI co-author trailers. ## Testing Verified authorship on all six landed contributor commits via git log (Alessandro Boni as author, Eduard only as committer), then exercised the product surface: the demo CLI run twice produces the four new Table 7 sections at exactly the 905 lines and md5 hash RESULTS.md claims, byte-identical between runs; the docs transcript test re-checks that output byte-for-byte, the 12 contributed tests and the HTML renderer test pass (48 passed total across the targeted modules), and PR 25's documented JSON-metrics recipe was run by hand and behaves as documented with null for unmeasured metrics. No visual artifact was captured because this change touches only the CLI demo, tests and Markdown docs — docs/index.html and the HTML renderer output are unchanged in the diff, and their byte-for-byte test still passes.

The line-count and md5 fields were updated, this one was not, so the file names a commit whose tree cannot produce the transcript it carries. `test_docs_example_output.py` does not check the captured-at commit, so nothing catches it. - ℹ️ `RESULTS.md:66` - "`reasonsmith`'s own test suite (`189 passed` on current suite...)" and the same figure at line 350 are stale after this branch adds 11 tests to `tests/test_reasonsmith.py`. items.title: Add 26 real CISI Operational Risk exam questions (April 2026)
items.body:
Adds all 26 questions from the CISI Operational Risk paper (April 19, 2026) to the question bank, tagged for filtering and covering all 7 chapters proportionally.

## Question bank (`js/questions.js`)
- Appended IDs 76–101 to the `QUESTIONS` array
- Each entry carries `previousExam: true`, `examDate: "April 2026"`, `chapter: <int>`, and `unit: "OR Chapter X"` for UI filtering
- Chapter distribution mirrors real exam weighting (Ch3 heaviest: 11 questions)

```js
{
  id: 76,
  unit: "OR Chapter 3",
  chapter: 3,
  topic: "Risk Appetite",
  question: "What would typically be included in a risk appetite statement ...",
  options: [ "A. A corrective action plan ...", "B. Ignore until next review", ... ],
  correct: 0,
  previousExam: true,
  examDate: "April 2026",
  explanation: "..."
}
```

## Coverage by chapter
| Chapter | IDs | Topics |
|---------|-----|--------|
| Ch1 — Risk Basics | 77, 94 | GAM incident, BIS/Basel definition |
| Ch2 — Other Major Risks | 82, 83, 86, 89 | Market depth, credit mitigation, VaR tail risk, credit rating agency failures |
| Ch3 — Nature of Operational Risk | 76, 78–80, 87–88, 90–91, 96–97, 101 | Risk appetite, loss data, reporting, 3LoD, benchmarking, heat map, 4Ts, KRIs, scenario analysis |
| Ch4 — Causes & Impacts | 81, 85 | Inaccurate reporting classification, near-miss recording |
| Ch5 — Trade Cycle | 93, 95, 100 | Corporate actions, legal stage, pre-settlement confirmation |
| Ch6 — Support & Control | 84, 99 | Merger integration, middle office reconciliation |
| Ch7 — Regulatory Environment | 92, 98 | Product suitability (MiFID II/COBS), Basel II Pillar 1 8% ratio |

## Minor UI/docs
- Homepage question count: `75+` → `100+`
- README "How to Add" example ID: `76` → `102`

<!-- START COPILOT ORIGINAL PROMPT -->



<details>

<summary>Original prompt</summary>


Add the following **real previous exam questions** from the CISI Operational Risk exam (April 19, 2026) into the question bank in `js/questions.js`. These must be added as high-quality multiple-choice questions alongside the existing question bank.

## Real Exam Questions to Add (April 19, 2026)

For each question below, create a realistic 4-option MCQ (A/B/C/D) with the correct answer and a detailed explanation referencing the relevant book chapter. Assign each to the correct chapter based on topic.

1. **"What would typically be included in a risk appetite statement to address a risk which has been assessed as exceeding risk appetite limits?"**
   - Chapter 3, topic: Risk Appetite
   - Correct answer: A specific action plan or remediation/escalation procedure outlining steps to reduce the risk back within appetite
   - Options should include: corrective action plan, ignore until next review, increase the risk limit to match current level, remove the risk from the register

2. **"How did the realisation of operational risk cause the regulator to suspend GAM's Absolute Return Fund in 2018?"**
   - Chapter 1, topic: Major Operational Risk Incidents
   - Correct: A whistleblower reported breaches of dealing, inducement and record-keeping policies leading to the fund suspension
   - Distractors: cyber attack on systems, fraudulent client accounts, failure of outsourced provider

3. **"Which of the following best describes historical loss data analysis?"**
   - Chapter 3, topic: Risk Measurement Methods
   - Correct: A review of past operational loss events to identify patterns, trends and potential future exposures
   - Distractors: forward-looking scenario analysis, assessment of market price movements, review of credit default rates

4. **"Which of these is a purpose of internal reporting of risk events?"**
   - Chapter 3, topic: Risk Reporting
   - Correct: To enable management to identify trends, escalate issues and make informed decisions on risk mitigation
   - Distractors: to satisfy only external regulatory requirements, to record events for insurance purposes only, to assign blame to individuals

5. **"A firm's internal audit function is important in terms of the operational risk management process because it:"**
   - Chapter 3, topic: Three Lines of Defence
   - Correct: Provides independent assurance on the effectiveness of risk management and internal controls (third line of defence)
   - Distractors: manages day-to-day operational risks, sets the firm's risk appetite, executes trades on behalf of clients

6. **"Inaccurate financial reporting can lead to poor decision-making and is classified as:"**
   - Chapter 4, topic: Causes and Impacts
   - Correct: An operational risk event arising from process failure
   - Distractors: a market risk event, a liquidity risk event, a credit risk event

7. **"Market depth is defined as the:"**
   - Chapter 2, topic: Market Risk / Liquidity
   - Correct: Ability of a market to absorb large trade volumes without significantly affecting the price
   - Distractors: total market capitalisation, number of market participants, volatility of asset prices

8. **"A common credit risk mitigation technique at the individual borrower level is:"**
   - Chapter 2, topic: Credit Risk Management
   - Correct: Requiring collateral or security against the loan
   - Distractors: diversifying the investment portfolio, increasing VaR limits, applying stress testing

9. **"For a successful merger between two major financial institutions, which function implements the integration?"**
   - Chapter 6, topic: Support and Control Functions
   - Correct: Operations / the operations function, as it manages the integration of systems, processes and people
   - Distractors: the front office trading desk, the compliance function alone, the external auditors

10. **"An error in a contract reads £1 million rather than £10 million but is corrected in time. What action is required?"**
    - Chapter 4, topic: Near Misses and Loss Event Recording
    - Correct: The error should be recorded as a near miss in the operational risk loss event database even though no financial loss occurred
    - Distractors: no action needed as no loss occurred, report immediately to the FCA, raise a formal complaint against the counterparty

11. **"Which of the following is a disadvantage of value-at-risk (VaR)? It does not:"**
    - Chapter 2, topic: Market Risk Measurement
    - Correct: Capture the size of losses beyond the confidence level (tail risk / extreme events)
    - Distractors: use statistical methods, apply to trading portfolios, consider historical price data

12. **"A firm has completed a risk measurement exercise using the benchmarking method. What will the results mainly indicate?"**
    - Chapter 3, topic: Risk Measurement Methods
    - Correct: How the firm's risk profile compares to industry peers or external data sources
    - Distractors: the exact capital required under Basel III, the precis...

</details>

items.title: fix: Step #4 — KV memory benchmark + honest correction of K4/V2 runtime memory claim
items.body:
## Summary

Step #4 from the v0.4-after roadmap: extend the long-context benchmark
to 100K+ tokens to validate the v0.3.1 K4/V2 memory savings at the
scale where they should matter most.

**The benchmark revealed a fundamental misframing in the v0.3.1 docs.**
K4/V2 KV cache quantization does **not** save peak runtime memory on
Apple Silicon. The 80% number is real for compressed-storage size, but
does not translate to runtime peak memory because the v0.3.1
incremental cache strategy holds a persistent dequantized buffer at
full input precision (the design choice that enables O(1) per-token
decode throughput).

This is the most important finding from the v0.4 cycle and it changes
how the project should be marketed. The PR ships the benchmark, the
finding writeup, and the corrected framing across README, paper,
and the where_tqai_shines report.

## What's in this PR

### New benchmark — `benchmarks/benchmark_kv_memory.py`

A subprocess-isolated KV cache memory benchmark using MLX-native
memory APIs (`mx.get_active_memory()`, `mx.get_peak_memory()`,
`mx.reset_peak_memory()`). Each (context, config) pair runs in its
own Python subprocess so MLX memory measurements are isolated and
the lifetime-max problem of `ru_maxrss` doesn't apply.

The first version of this script had two measurement bugs that I
caught and fixed:
1. Used `resource.getrusage(...).ru_maxrss` which is the lifetime
   max RSS — once the first config peaks, all subsequent reads
   report that peak even if memory has been freed.
2. The decode tokens/sec calculation subtracted prefill_time from
   generation_time, which gives near-zero (clamped) on the second
   `mlx_lm.generate()` call due to mlx-lm's internal caching.

Both fixed by switching to subprocess isolation + MLX-native memory
APIs + measuring prefill and decode in separate phases with explicit
reset_peak_memory() between them.

### The result — `reports/kv_memory_finding.md` and the JSON

Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct-8bit, default `cache_strategy="incremental"`:

| Context | Baseline KV | tqai K4/V2 KV | Δ |
|--------:|------------:|--------------:|--:|
| 4 K | 0.87 GB | 0.90 GB | **−0.03 GB** |
| 32 K | 2.41 GB | 2.56 GB | **−0.16 GB** |
| 64 K | 4.35 GB | 4.45 GB | **−0.10 GB** |
| 128 K | 8.37 GB | 8.56 GB | **−0.19 GB** |

Negative Δ = tqai uses MORE memory. The pattern is consistent and
structural, cross-validated with two independent measurement
methodologies (subprocess + `mlx_lm.generate` and direct
`model(ids, cache=cache)` with the cache held alive); both agree
within ±0.1 GB.

### Why this happens

`src/tqai/cache/mlx.py` lines 75-77 and 178-180:

```python
# Incremental dequantized buffer (strategies: incremental, residual)
self._k_buffer: Any | None = None  # [1, H, seq, D] in input dtype
self._v_buffer: Any | None = None

# ... in _update_incremental:
self._k_buffer = k_dequant   # full-precision tensor stored permanently
self._v_buffer = v_dequant
```

When a new prefill batch arrives:
1. Original input KV tensors (~size N)
2. tqai quantizes → compressed indices (~N/5)
3. tqai immediately dequantizes → STORES result in `_k_buffer` /
   `_v_buffer` (~N) — this enables O(1) per-token decode
4. Compressed indices are also kept (~N/5)
5. Plus rotation matrices and codebooks (~tens of MB / layer)

At the peak: ~1.2N + constant overhead. Baseline is just N. The
compressed storage exists IN ADDITION to the dequantized buffer,
not instead of it. **This is by design** — it's the v0.3.1 design
choice to trade runtime memory for throughput. KIVI (cited in
`cache/mlx.py:8`) makes the same trade-off. KVQuant (also cited)
shows that the actual unlock is a fused dequant-attention kernel
that computes Q·Kᵀ directly on compressed K/V without materializing
the full bf16 tensors.

### What the v0.3.1 K4/V2 win actually IS

1. **Quality preservation** (still valid). Δppl = 0.00 across every
   model and quantization config we tested. Output is byte-identical
   to baseline.
2. **Compressed-storage size** (still valid). 5x reduction for
   serialized KV cache, useful for offline workflows and as the
   prerequisite for a future fused kernel.
3. **Foundation for a future fused dequant-attention Metal kernel**
   (potential, on the v0.5 roadmap).

### What it is NOT

A peak runtime memory win on Apple Silicon. The README, paper, and
several reports stated or implied this. This PR corrects all three.

### Documentation corrections

- **README**: replaced "80%+ memory savings" with "byte-identical
  output to baseline" + multi-paragraph honest framing callout.
  Renamed "Memory Saved" column to "Compressed-Storage Saved" with
  explicit note that it's not a peak runtime reduction.
- **paper/tqai_paper.md and .tex**: abstract reframed from "80% KV
  cache memory savings" to "80% reduction in compressed-storage KV
  cache size". Conclusion expanded from "two principled negative
  results" to "three", with the full measurement table inline.
  Future-work item swapped: removed the now-obsolete "long-context
  KV memory benchmark" item (done in §10.7), added "fused
  dequant-attention Metal kernel" as the new high-priority unlock.
- **reports/where_tqai_shines.md**: split the single KV cache
  quantization row into two — quality (Ship it) and peak runtime
  memory (Honest negative result).
- **reports/kv_memory_finding.md** (new): full writeup of the
  finding, the explanation, the implications, and the proposed
  next steps.

### Test count update

447 → 467. The 20 new tests came from the Step #1 video presets PR
(merged earlier today). Step #4 doesn't add tests because the
benchmark script doesn't expose new APIs — it uses existing
`tqai.patch()` and `mlx_lm.generate()`.

## Test plan

- [x] All 467 tests pass on macOS
- [x] `ruff check .` clean
- [x] LaTeX environment balance verified
- [x] Benchmark runs end-to-end at 4K, 32K, 64K, 128K context on
      Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct-8bit
- [x] Cross-validation with direct `model(ids, cache=cache)` test
      confirms the same conclusion (tqai within ±0.1 GB of baseline)
- [ ] CI green (will run on push)

## What this PR does NOT include

- A fused dequant-attention Metal kernel (the actual unlock — that's
  a v0.5 research project, 1-2 weeks of Metal shader work).
- Step #2 (`mx.compile` CFG sharing) — separate decision needed about
  whether it's worth pursuing given the Step #4 finding suggests the
  whole "Python overhead is the bottleneck" framing was wrong.
- Step #3 (offline Fisher calibration) — still valid, but lower
  priority now that the headline correction is the more important
  fix.
- Step #5 (preset system for LLM patching) — depends on having
  concrete recommendations to present, which now need to be redesigned
  around what tqai actually does (quality preservation, compressed
  storage for offline workflows, video pipelines).

## Why I think this is the most important PR in the v0.4 cycle

The whole point of the v0.4 work was to be honest about what tqai
actually delivers locally on Apple Silicon. We shipped reference
implementations of 12 papers, validated some, found principled
negative results for others. Step #4 found that the **headline claim
of the entire project was framed wrong**. Correcting it is more
valuable than any individual feature would have been, because
otherwise users would expect memory savings that don't materialize
and walk away disappointed.

The K4/V2 quantization is still useful — quality preservation is real,
the compressed-storage form is real, the foundation for a future
fused kernel is real. But the marketing needs to match what the system
actually does today, not what we hoped it would do.

items.title: WMMA prefill pipeline — GEMM + FlashAttention on gfx1201 (Phase 2 + 3)
items.body:
## Summary

Full WMMA-based prefill pipeline for RDNA 4 (gfx1201). The prefill path now dispatches hand-written `__builtin_amdgcn_wmma_f32_16x16x16_f16_w32_gfx12` kernels for both Q4_0 GEMM projections and FlashAttention, and runs on prompts of **any** length via zero-padding of the activation scratch.

This PR closes out the prefill-optimization arc: Phase 1 (hipBLAS reference baseline, subsequently bypassed), Phase 2 (WMMA GEMM), Phase 3 (WMMA attention + GQA + causal mask), Phase 3.1 (padding for arbitrary `seq_len ≥ 64`), and Phase 3.2 (threshold lowered to `seq_len ≥ 1`).

## Measured impact (RX 9070 XT / gfx1201 / ROCm 7.2.1 / Qwen2.5-7B Q4_0)

### 15-prompt real-world benchmark (5 code / 5 chat / 5 prose, median of 3)

| Metric | Before this PR | After this PR | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Prefill tok/s (median) | 60.6 | **356** | **5.9×** |
| TTFT (ms, median) | 396 | **67** | **5.9× faster** |
| Decode tok/s (median) | 102 | 102 | ±0 (prefill-only path) |
| Wall-clock, 24 prompt + 128 gen (ms, median) | 1,648 | **1,319** | 20 % shorter |

### llama.cpp ROCm head-to-head (same host, `build 408225b`)

| Metric | ROCmForge | llama.cpp | Ratio |
|--------|----------:|----------:|------:|
| Decode (tok/s) | 102 | 121 | 0.84× |
| Prefill real prompts (median, tok/s) | 356 | 526 | 0.68× |
| Prefill pp256 synthetic (tok/s) | 620 | 4,951 | 0.13× |
| Prefill pp512 synthetic (tok/s) | 629 | 5,158 | 0.12× |
| Wall-clock real prompts (median, ms) | 1,319 | 1,104 | 1.20× |

Synthetic long-prompt prefill looks bad in isolation (0.12–0.13×) but the wall-clock gap on realistic prompts is only 1.20×. The remaining synthetic gap is **not** a kernel-performance issue — isolated WMMA GEMM sits at 62–75 % of FP16 peak and isolated WMMA attention is 355× faster than the scalar kernel at pp=256. The gap is ~295 ms of unfused norm / RoPE / residual / embedding overhead at pp=256 on the prefill path; llama.cpp fuses more of this. That is the next target.

### Synthetic pp sweep (ROCmForge only)

| pp | Custom GEMM | hipBLAS | WMMA GEMM only | WMMA GEMM + Attn |
|---:|------------:|--------:|---------------:|-----------------:|
|  64 | 62 | 77 | 89 | **560** |
| 128 | 63 | 82 | 90 | **602** |
| 256 | 64 | 86 | 92 | **620** |
| 512 | 50 | 63 | 67 | **629** |

### Isolated attention kernel (pp=256, Qwen2.5-7B shape)

| Scalar reference | WMMA + GQA + causal | Speedup |
|-----------------:|--------------------:|--------:|
| 78,412 µs | 221 µs | **355×** |

## What changed

### Kernels (HIP)

- `hip_kernels/wmma/wmma_gemm_16x16.hip` — single 16×16 WMMA proof-of-concept, bit-identical to CPU FP32 on three diagnostic cases.
- `hip_kernels/wmma/wmma_gemm_tiled.hip` — tiled 64×64 FP16→FP32 WMMA GEMM, 2.96–3.40× vs. hipBLAS on three Qwen2.5-7B projection shapes, 62–75 % of FP16 peak.
- `hip_kernels/wmma/wmma_gemm_q4_0.hip` — inline Q4_0 dequant in the K-loop (no FP16 weight scratch round-trip), bit-identical to the separate-dequant + Phase 2a GEMM path, 2.5× vs. hipBLAS on isolated GEMM, 28–36 % over Phase 2a.
- `hip_kernels/wmma/wmma_attention_prefill.hip` — FlashAttention-style online softmax with 64×64 Q/KV tiling, GQA (separate `q_row_stride` / `kv_row_stride`, `kv_head = q_head / gqa_ratio`), and causal masking with zero-work elimination for upper-triangle tiles plus per-element diagonal masking. Baked in `head_dim = 128`.

### Dispatch (Rust)

- `src/gpu/ops.rs` — `gpu_dispatch_gemm` prefers WMMA for Q4_0 tensors when `seq_len ≥ 1 && out_dim % 64 == 0 && in_dim % 32 == 0 && !needs_transpose`. Dispatch order: WMMA → hipBLAS → custom GEMM → batched/tiled GEMV.
- `src/gpu/forward.rs` — `gpu_attention_prefill` replaces the scalar per-head loop with one WMMA dispatch when `seq_len ≥ 1 && head_dim == 128 && num_heads % num_kv_heads == 0`. FP32 → FP16 activation conversion runs on the same stream; FP16 staging buffers are lazily allocated and zero-initialised once.
- `src/gpu/cache.rs` — `GpuPrefillScratch` always pads `buffer_seq_len` to a multiple of 64 (minimum 64 rows) and zero-initialises the activation buffers once. Padding rows stay zero through the forward pass (GEMM-of-zero is zero; the causal mask filters padding K positions from real queries). `decode_scratch.logits_batch` oversized to 64 rows so the batched verify lm_head can safely dispatch at `padded_M = 64` without OOB.
- `src/gpu/safety.rs` — new opt-out flags `ROCMFORGE_DISABLE_WMMA_PREFILL=1` and `ROCMFORGE_DISABLE_WMMA_ATTENTION=1`.

### Correctness

- `tests/wmma_attention_gqa_causal_correctness.rs` — 9 scenarios (GQA-only, causal-only, GQA + causal) across `seq ∈ {64, 128, 256}`, `max_abs_diff` 8.9e-6 to 3.5e-5 at tol 1e-2, plus bit-exact `O[0] = V[0]` check across all 28 heads.
- `tests/wmma_padding_correctness.rs` — 6 scenarios for unaligned `seq_len` {65, 100, 200, 300} and aligned no-op checks {64, 128}; first decoded token must match the scalar fallback.
- `tests/prefill_wmma_attention_e2e.rs` — end-to-end first-decoded-token equivalence vs. the scalar attention kernel on an 80-word prompt.
- `tests/prefill_wmma_matches_hipblas.rs` — WMMA GEMM path produces the same first decoded token as the hipBLAS reference.
- `tests/prefill_hipblas_matches_gemv.rs` — hipBLAS prefill path matches the custom GEMV reference.
- All existing GPU regression suites (`spec_greedy_matches_baseline`, 3 depths) still pass.

## Hardware support

**RDNA 4 (gfx1201) only.** All kernels use `__builtin_amdgcn_wmma_f32_16x16x16_f16_w32_gfx12`, which is gfx12-specific. Porting to RDNA 3 (gfx1100) is **not** a flag change — it needs a different intrinsic name (no `_gfx12` suffix), a different A/B matrix register layout (8 VGPRs instead of 4 with a duplication pattern), lane duplication (lanes 0–15 → 16–31), and re-deriving the output lane-to-row/column mapping from the AMD matrix-instruction calculator. README now documents this explicitly; the previous "Tested on RDNA 3 (RX 7900 XT, gfx1100)" line was never accurate and has been removed.

## Docs

- `README.md` — complete rewrite of Performance, Supported hardware, Limitations sections with measured numbers. Removed the false RDNA 3 claim, replaced stale baselines (82 → 102 tok/s decode), added honest llama.cpp head-to-head (both perspectives: synthetic and real), corrected speculative-decode framing (is a loss at greedy on every real prompt, not a code-generation win).
- `docs/architecture_notes.md` — new "WMMA intrinsics — RDNA 4 (gfx12) only" section enumerating what a gfx11 port would require.
- `CHANGELOG.md` — entries for each phase from Phase 2a through Phase 3.2.
- `benches/results/` — raw JSON + analysis docs for every measurement:
  - `prefill_wmma_e2e_analysis.md` (Phase 2d)
  - `prefill_wmma_attn_e2e_analysis.md` (Phase 3d + llama.cpp head-to-head)
  - `full_benchmark_wmma_analysis.md` (15-prompt real benchmark, Phase 3.2 update inline)
- `profiling/results/wmma_*_analysis.md` — per-kernel analyses.

## What is explicitly not in this PR

- Fusion of `norm + QKV + RoPE` on the prefill path (decode path already has it). This is the ~295 ms residual overhead that keeps the synthetic pp=256 gap at ~8×.
- Explicit LDS KV sharing across Q heads in attention (measured as not needed — L2 covers it, attention is now < 2 % of pp=256 prefill).
- WMMA on non-Q4_0 quantisation formats.
- Rejection-sampling speculative decode (would make spec-decode a win on lower-α workloads).
- Any RDNA 3 / RDNA 2 / CDNA port.

## Test plan

- [ ] `cargo build --release --features gpu` on an RDNA 4 host
- [ ] `cargo test --release --features gpu -- --test-threads=1` — CPU unit tests + GPU integration tests
- [ ] `ROCMFORGE_RUN_REAL_MODEL_GPU_TESTS=1 cargo test --release --features gpu --test wmma_padding_correctness --test prefill_wmma_attention_e2e --test prefill_wmma_matches_hipblas --test wmma_attention_gqa_causal_correctness -- --test-threads=1`
- [ ] `ROCMFORGE_RUN_REAL_MODEL_GPU_TESTS=1 cargo test --release --features gpu --test spec_greedy_matches_baseline -- --ignored --test-threads=1`
- [ ] Spot-check end-to-end: `./target/release/rocmforge --model ~/models/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf --prompt "Hello" --max-tokens 16 --gpu --temperature 0.0 --top-p 1.0 --no-template`
- [ ] Run the real-prompt benchmark: `fish benches/bench_full_15prompts.fish`
- [ ] Confirm decode throughput is unchanged with a baseline decode run (should land at ~102 tok/s on 7B Q4_0 greedy)
